simple.1.1: The blind king Dhritarashtra asks his advisor Sanjaya what happened when both armies gathered at Kurukshetra. The Gita opens with a worried question from someone who cannot see, setting up a story about learning to see clearly.
simple.1.2: Sanjaya reports that Prince Duryodhana, seeing the Pandava army lined up, hurried over to his teacher Drona. His rush hints at the nervousness hiding behind his confident front.
simple.1.3: Duryodhana points out that the Pandava army is arranged by Drupada's son, who was Drona's own student. There is a sharp edge here: he is hinting that Drona trained his enemy.
simple.1.4: Duryodhana starts listing the mighty archers on the other side, comparing them to Bhima and Arjuna. Naming his rivals one by one shows how heavily they weigh on his mind.
simple.1.5: The list of opposing heroes continues with more kings and champions. Duryodhana keeps counting the strengths of others, a sign of his growing worry.
simple.1.6: More famous fighters are named, including Abhimanyu (Subhadra's son) and the sons of Draupadi. The list makes clear how strong and united the Pandava side is.
simple.1.7: Duryodhana turns to his own side and offers to name his leading generals for Drona. He seems to be reassuring himself as much as informing his teacher.
simple.1.8: He names his top commanders: Drona himself, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashwatthama, Vikarna and the son of Somadatta. They are great warriors, yet his anxiety does not settle.
simple.1.9: Duryodhana says many other heroes are ready to give their lives for him, all well armed and skilled. He leans on the loyalty of others to feel secure.
simple.1.10: Duryodhana compares the two armies, one guarded by Bhishma and the other by Bhima. Translators differ on whether he calls his own force unlimited or insufficient, but either way his words carry unease beneath the boast.
simple.1.11: He orders all his commanders to hold their positions and, above all, to protect Bhishma. Worry makes him focus on guarding his main source of support.
simple.1.12: To cheer Duryodhana up, the elder Bhishma blows his conch shell with a sound like a lion's roar. It is a loud signal that the battle is about to begin.
simple.1.13: At once, conches, drums, cymbals and horns sound all around in a huge uproar. The noise shows how charged and tense the moment has become.
simple.1.14: From their great chariot drawn by white horses, Krishna and Arjuna blow their divine conch shells. Their answer rises clearly from the side where Krishna stands.
simple.1.15: Krishna blows his conch Panchajanya, Arjuna blows Devadatta, and Bhima blows the mighty Paundra. Each conch has a name, as each hero steps forward to be counted.
simple.1.16: King Yudhishthira blows Anantavijaya, while Nakula and Sahadeva blow Sughosha and Manipushpaka. The whole Pandava family answers the call together.
simple.1.17: Allies such as the king of Kashi, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata and the unconquered Satyaki join in. Many people are now committed to the coming battle.
simple.1.18: Drupada, the sons of Draupadi and the mighty Abhimanyu also blow their conches. Every leader on the Pandava side has now declared readiness.
simple.1.19: The roar of the Pandava conches echoes through earth and sky and shakes the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons. The sound reveals the fear hidden on the Kaurava side.
simple.1.20: Arjuna, whose flag bears the image of Hanuman, sees the Kaurava army standing ready and lifts his bow. He is poised at the very edge of action.
simple.1.21: Arjuna asks Krishna, who is driving his chariot, to place it between the two armies. The image of Krishna as charioteer becomes a picture of a wise guide steering us where we need to look.
simple.1.22: Arjuna wants to see clearly who has come to fight and whom he must face. It is an honest wish to look straight at what lies ahead before acting.
simple.1.23: He wants to see those who have gathered to please Duryodhana, whose mind is set on wrong. At this point Arjuna still sees the battle as simple and clear-cut.
simple.1.24: Sanjaya says Krishna, hearing Arjuna's request, drives the splendid chariot into the space between both armies. Krishna does exactly what is asked and lets Arjuna see for himself.
simple.1.25: Facing Bhishma, Drona and the other kings, Krishna says, 'Arjuna, look at all these Kurus gathered here.' This simple 'look' sets off Arjuna's crisis, because he now sees family, not just opponents.
simple.1.26: Arjuna sees fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends standing in the ranks. The 'enemy' suddenly has familiar, beloved faces.
simple.1.27: He sees fathers-in-law and well-wishers in both armies. Looking at all his relatives gathered for war, his heart begins to give way.
simple.1.28: Overcome with deep pity, Arjuna speaks sadly to Krishna about seeing his own people eager to fight. Compassion and grief start to flood him.
simple.1.29: Arjuna's limbs go weak, his mouth goes dry, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. The Gita honestly shows how strong emotion hits the body first.
simple.1.30: His bow slips from his hand, his skin burns, and his mind spins so that he can barely stand. Even the greatest archer can be overwhelmed.
simple.1.31: Arjuna sees bad omens and can find no good in killing his own family. His distress is now shaping how he reads everything around him.
simple.1.32: Arjuna says he wants no victory, kingdom or pleasure if it costs his loved ones. What use would a kingdom, or even life, be without them?
simple.1.33: The very people he would want to share success with are standing here, ready to give up their wealth and lives. Winning starts to feel empty.
simple.1.34: He lists teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, uncles, in-laws and other relatives. Arjuna keeps naming each relationship, and each one deepens his pain.
simple.1.35: Arjuna says he would not kill them even to rule three worlds, let alone this earth, even if they kill him. His love is real, though his thinking is growing clouded.
simple.1.36: He asks what joy could come from killing Dhritarashtra's sons, and fears that even fighting wrongdoers would bring sin upon him. He is searching for a moral way out.
simple.1.37: Arjuna says it is not right to kill their own relatives, for how could they ever be happy afterwards? He is measuring the choice by the sorrow he expects to feel.
simple.1.38: Arjuna notes that the other side, blinded by greed, sees nothing wrong in destroying family or betraying friends. He sees their fault very clearly.
simple.1.39: He asks why he, who can see the wrong in destroying a family, should not turn away from it. His reasoning sounds wise, yet it is coming from grief.
simple.1.40: Arjuna worries that when families are destroyed, their long-held traditions fade and disorder takes over the home. He fears losing what holds a family together.
simple.1.41: He fears that once these values collapse, family life breaks down and the social order of his time gets mixed up. These are his era's worries, voiced in his grief.
simple.1.42: Arjuna says such a breakdown harms both the family and those who cause it, and even the ancestors lose their honored rituals. He feels the war's damage reaching across generations.
simple.1.43: He repeats that those who destroy families also wipe out the long-standing duties of community and family. Arjuna is piling up reasons, and each one adds to his fear.
simple.1.44: Arjuna says he has heard that people whose family traditions are destroyed suffer for a very long time. He leans on what he has heard to support his doubts.
simple.1.45: He cries out that it is strange and sad that they were ready to commit such a great wrong just for the pleasures of a kingdom. He is shocked at himself.
simple.1.46: Arjuna says it would be better if he were killed unarmed and unresisting. This shows how deep his despair has gone: he would rather give up than act.
simple.1.47: Arjuna sets down his bow and arrows and sinks into the seat of his chariot, overwhelmed with grief. The chapter ends at his lowest point, which is exactly where real guidance begins.
simple.2.1: Sanjaya describes Arjuna in tears, overcome with pity and despair, as Krishna begins to speak. The Gita's teaching starts by meeting someone exactly where they are hurting.
simple.2.2: Krishna asks why this gloom has come over Arjuna at such a crucial moment, saying it doesn't suit a noble person or lead anywhere good. His firm tone comes from believing in Arjuna.
simple.2.3: Krishna urges Arjuna not to give in to faint-heartedness, but to shake off this weakness and stand up. It is a strong wake-up call to someone he knows is capable.
simple.2.4: Arjuna replies that he cannot shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, elders he deeply honors. His conflict between duty and reverence is real and painful.
simple.2.5: Arjuna says he would rather live by begging than kill his honored teachers, because any gain would feel stained with their blood. He is torn between love and duty.
simple.2.6: Arjuna admits he doesn't even know which outcome would be better, winning or losing. Not knowing what you even want is a sign of a truly confused mind.
simple.2.7: Arjuna admits he is confused about his dharma (rightful duty) and asks Krishna to teach him as his student. This humble request turns friendship into a teacher-student bond, and the real teaching begins.
simple.2.8: Arjuna says that not even a rich kingdom on earth or rule over the gods could remove the grief drying up his senses. He sees that no outer gain can heal an inner wound.
simple.2.9: Arjuna tells Krishna, 'I will not fight,' and falls silent. He has reached the end of his own answers.
simple.2.10: Krishna, with a gentle smile, speaks to the grieving Arjuna between the two armies. His smile shows calm, warmth and confidence that there is a way through.
simple.2.11: Krishna says Arjuna speaks words that sound wise, yet grieves for what does not call for grief. The wise do not mourn for the living or the dead, because they see what truly lasts.
simple.2.12: Krishna says there was never a time when he, Arjuna or these kings did not exist, and there never will be. Our deepest self is not limited to this one life.
simple.2.13: Just as the self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, it passes into another body at death. The wise are not shaken by this change.
simple.2.14: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain arise when the senses meet the world, and they come and go. Since they don't last, Krishna asks Arjuna to bear them patiently.
simple.2.15: A person who stays steady through pleasure and pain, and is not thrown off by them, is ready for lasting freedom. Steadiness is the doorway to deep peace.
simple.2.16: What is unreal has no lasting existence, and what is real never stops existing. The wise learn to tell the passing from the lasting.
simple.2.17: The spirit that pervades everything can never be destroyed. Nothing has the power to wipe out what is truly eternal.
simple.2.18: Bodies come to an end, but the self living in them is eternal and beyond measure. So Krishna tells Arjuna to take up his duty and fight.
simple.2.19: Whoever thinks the self is a killer, or thinks it can be killed, does not understand. The true self neither kills nor is killed.
simple.2.20: The self is never born and never dies; it did not come into being and will not stop being. It is eternal and ancient, and it is not destroyed when the body is.
simple.2.21: Someone who knows the self as indestructible, eternal, unborn and unchanging sees that it cannot truly kill or be killed. This understanding goes to the root of Arjuna's fear.
simple.2.22: Just as we set aside worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. Death is a change, not the end of who we are.
simple.2.23: Weapons cannot cut the self, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, and wind cannot dry it. Nothing physical can touch who you really are.
simple.2.24: The self cannot be cut, burned, soaked or dried. It is eternal, present everywhere, steady, unmoving and ancient.
simple.2.25: The self cannot be seen by the eyes or fully grasped by the mind, and it never changes. Knowing this, there is no reason to grieve.
simple.2.26: Krishna adds that even if Arjuna believes the self is constantly born and constantly dies, he still has no reason to grieve like this. Either way, endless sorrow does not help.
simple.2.27: Death is certain for everyone who is born, and birth follows death. Grieving over what cannot be avoided only adds to our pain.
simple.2.28: Beings are unseen before birth and after death, and visible only in between. Seeing life this way can soften our grief over endings.
simple.2.29: Some see the self as a wonder, some speak of it as a wonder, some hear of it as a wonder, yet few truly understand it. Deep truths take time to sink in.
simple.2.30: The self living in every body is eternal and can never be harmed. So Arjuna need not grieve for any living being.
simple.2.31: Krishna now turns to Arjuna's own dharma (rightful duty) as a warrior: for him, nothing is better than a fight for what is right. Duty, too, asks him not to waver.
simple.2.32: Krishna says fortunate are warriors who get such a chance to fight for what is right, as if an open door to heaven had come to them. A meaningful challenge can be a gift.
simple.2.33: Krishna says that if Arjuna refuses this righteous battle, he would be turning away from his duty and his honor, and doing wrong. Avoiding what is truly ours to do has a cost.
simple.2.34: Krishna says people will speak of Arjuna's dishonor for a long time, and for someone respected, that feels worse than death. He is appealing to Arjuna's deep sense of honor.
simple.2.35: The great warriors who now respect Arjuna would think he left the battle out of fear. Krishna points out that others would see only retreat, not compassion.
simple.2.36: Krishna says Arjuna's opponents would mock his courage with harsh words, and asks what could be more painful. He is using Arjuna's own values to rouse him.
simple.2.37: Whether Arjuna falls or wins, he gains something: heaven or the kingdom. So Krishna urges him to rise and fight with resolve.
simple.2.38: Treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, and then act; this way you will not incur wrong. Acting from an even mind is at the heart of the Gita.
simple.2.39: Krishna says he has explained the wisdom of the self, and now he will teach the yoga of action (karma yoga). Practiced with understanding, it frees a person from the bondage that actions create.
simple.2.40: On this path, no effort is ever wasted and nothing goes backward. Even a little practice protects a person from great fear.
simple.2.41: On this path, the mind is resolute, with one clear aim. An unsettled mind splits off in endless directions.
simple.2.42: Krishna says people with limited understanding get caught up in the flowery promises of scripture about rewards, and claim there is nothing beyond them. Attractive promises can distract from real growth.
simple.2.43: Driven by desire, such people focus on rituals for pleasure, power and heavenly rewards. Krishna points out that this keeps them going round in circles of birth and action.
simple.2.44: Those attached to pleasure and power have their minds carried away, so they cannot settle into steady, focused wisdom. Chasing comforts scatters attention.
simple.2.45: The Vedas deal with the three gunas (qualities of nature). Krishna asks Arjuna to rise above them, free from the pull of opposites, steady and grounded in the self.
simple.2.46: For someone who truly knows, the scriptures' rituals serve no more purpose than a small well in a land flooded with water. Inner wisdom already includes what those rituals aim for.
simple.2.47: You have a right to do your work, but not to control its results. Don't let results be your motive, and don't slip into doing nothing either. This is one of the Gita's most famous lessons.
simple.2.48: Do your work steadily, letting go of clinging and staying even in success and failure. This evenness of mind is what yoga truly means.
simple.2.49: Krishna says acting only for reward is far below acting with a wise, steady mind, so take refuge in that wisdom. Those driven only by results stay anxious and poor in spirit.
simple.2.50: A person with this wisdom lets go of both good and bad results, even in this life. So devote yourself to yoga, for yoga is skill in action.
simple.2.51: The wise, by letting go of the fruits of their actions, become free from the cycle of birth and reach a state beyond sorrow.
simple.2.52: When your understanding climbs out of the swamp of confusion, you stop being swayed by everything you have heard or will hear. Clarity frees you from chasing every opinion.
simple.2.53: When your mind is no longer pulled around by conflicting teachings and rests steady in deep focus, you have reached yoga.
simple.2.54: Arjuna asks how to recognize a person of steady wisdom: how do they speak, sit and move? He wants to know what this looks like in daily life.
simple.2.55: Krishna says a person of steady wisdom has let go of the cravings of the mind and is content within themselves. Inner contentment is the first sign.
simple.2.56: One who is not shaken by sorrow, does not crave pleasures, and is free from attachment, fear and anger is called a sage of steady mind.
simple.2.57: Someone who is not bound by attachment, who neither gets carried away by good fortune nor hates bad fortune, has steady wisdom.
simple.2.58: Like a tortoise drawing its limbs into its shell, the wise can pull their senses back from distractions. This is a mark of steady wisdom.
simple.2.59: Holding back from pleasures can stop the action, but the taste for them lingers. That inner craving fades when one experiences something higher.
simple.2.60: The senses are so powerful that they can drag away the mind of even a wise person who is trying hard. Krishna is honest that self-control is not easy.
simple.2.61: Krishna says to restrain the senses and focus the mind on him, the highest. One whose senses are under control has steady wisdom.
simple.2.62: Dwelling on things you desire creates attachment; attachment grows into craving; and frustrated craving turns into anger. Our thoughts quietly shape where we end up.
simple.2.63: Anger brings confusion, confusion clouds memory, lost memory ruins judgment, and when judgment is lost, a person falls. Small thoughts can lead to big mistakes.
simple.2.64: Someone who moves among the things of the world with self-control, free from both craving and aversion, finds calm and clarity.
simple.2.65: In that calm, sorrows fade, and the mind soon becomes steady and clear.
simple.2.66: Without a steady, disciplined mind there is no clear understanding or inner focus; without that, no peace; and without peace, how can there be happiness?
simple.2.67: Just as a strong wind pushes a boat off course on the water, a mind that follows the wandering senses carries good judgment away.
simple.2.68: So, a person whose senses are held back from chasing their objects has steady wisdom.
simple.2.69: What is night to most beings, the wise are awake to; and what most are awake to, the wise see as night. They value differently what the world chases.
simple.2.70: The ocean stays steady while rivers keep flowing in. In the same way, the person who stays undisturbed as desires come finds peace, not the one who chases every desire.
simple.2.71: One who lets go of cravings and lives free of longing, without the sense of 'mine' and without ego, finds peace.
simple.2.72: This is the divine state; reaching it, one is no longer deluded. Resting in it even at the end of life, one attains lasting freedom and union with the divine.
simple.3.1: Arjuna is puzzled: if Krishna says wisdom matters more than action, why push him into a hard, painful fight? It is the honest question of anyone who would rather think than face a difficult task.
simple.3.2: Arjuna admits he feels confused and asks for one clear path to what is truly good for him. Asking for clarity when you are torn is the first step to finding it.
simple.3.3: Krishna explains there are two paths: the path of knowledge for those suited to reflection, and the path of action for those suited to work. Both are valid ways to grow.
simple.3.4: Simply avoiding work does not make you free, and giving things up on the surface does not make you wise. Freedom comes from how you act, not from refusing to act.
simple.3.5: No one can stay completely still, even for a moment; our very nature keeps us moving, breathing and thinking. Since action is unavoidable, the real question is how to act well.
simple.3.6: A person who holds back their body but keeps daydreaming about pleasures is fooling themselves. Outward restraint without inner change is only a show.
simple.3.7: Far better is the person who guides their senses with a steady mind and does their work without clinging to it. This is karma yoga (the path of selfless action).
simple.3.8: Do the work that is yours to do; acting is better than doing nothing. Even keeping your body alive needs effort, so action is simply part of life.
simple.3.9: Work done only for selfish gain ties us up; work done as yajna (an offering for a higher purpose) sets us free. So act without clinging, as a gift.
simple.3.10: At the beginning, the Creator made people along with the spirit of offering and said that by giving, they would flourish. Generosity is built into how life is meant to work.
simple.3.11: Honor the powers of nature that sustain you, and they will sustain you in return. When everyone supports one another, everyone thrives.
simple.3.12: Nature and the world give us so much; enjoying it all while giving nothing back is like taking without paying. The verse invites us to live with gratitude and give back.
simple.3.13: Those who share first and then enjoy what remains are freed from wrongdoing; those who cook only for themselves feed their own selfishness. Sharing purifies how we enjoy.
simple.3.14: Living beings depend on food, food on rain, rain on offering, and offering on action. Everything is linked in one great cycle of giving.
simple.3.15: All right action has its source in the Divine, which is eternal and present everywhere. So the Divine is especially present in acts of offering and service.
simple.3.16: Someone who refuses to take part in this cycle of giving, living only for their own pleasure, wastes the gift of life. Our lives gain meaning by contributing.
simple.3.17: A person who has found deep joy and contentment within the Self (their true inner being) no longer acts out of need. They feel complete inside.
simple.3.18: Such a person gains nothing personally from acting or not acting, and does not depend on anyone for their happiness. Their peace comes from within.
simple.3.19: So keep doing what needs to be done, without clinging to the outcome. Working this way, with a free heart, leads a person to the highest goal.
simple.3.20: King Janaka and other wise people reached perfection while fully engaged in action. Even just to set a good example and help the world, it is worth acting.
simple.3.21: People copy what respected people do; the standard they set becomes the one others follow. Our example quietly shapes those around us.
simple.3.22: Krishna says there is nothing he needs to do or gain, yet he keeps acting. Even one who needs nothing still chooses to work for the good of others.
simple.3.23: If Krishna stopped acting, people everywhere would follow his example and stop too. Leaders and role models carry extra responsibility to keep showing up.
simple.3.24: If Krishna stopped working, the world would fall into confusion and disorder. Steady, responsible action holds the world together.
simple.3.25: Unwise people work hard because they are attached to results; the wise should work just as hard, but without attachment, for the good of everyone.
simple.3.26: A wise person should not confuse or discourage those who are still working out of attachment. Better to inspire them by doing their own work well and with devotion.
simple.3.27: All actions are carried out by the forces of nature, the gunas (qualities of nature). Only the ego, confused, believes 'I alone am the doer.'
simple.3.28: One who understands how these qualities of nature interact sees that senses are simply responding to their objects. Seeing this, they stop clinging to their actions.
simple.3.29: People caught up in these qualities get attached to what they do. The wise should be patient with them rather than unsettling them before they are ready.
simple.3.30: Krishna invites Arjuna to offer all his actions to him, keep his mind on the Self, and act free from craving, ego and anxious agitation. Then he can face his task calmly.
simple.3.31: Those who practice this teaching with trust and without fault-finding are freed from the bonds that actions create. Practice, not just belief, brings freedom.
simple.3.32: Those who mock this teaching and ignore it lose their way, lacking understanding and good judgment. Rejecting wisdom leaves a person confused and lost.
simple.3.33: Even wise people act according to their nature, and all beings follow theirs. Simply forcing or suppressing ourselves does not work; nature has to be understood and guided.
simple.3.34: Liking and disliking naturally arise when our senses meet the world. The point is not to let them run our lives, because they block our path.
simple.3.35: It is better to do your own work imperfectly than someone else's work perfectly. Following your own true path is safer than living a life that is not yours.
simple.3.36: Arjuna asks what pushes people to do wrong even when they do not want to, as if forced. It is a deeply human question about why we act against our better judgment.
simple.3.37: Krishna answers: it is desire, and anger that grows from blocked desire, born of restless passion. Never fully satisfied, it is the real enemy to watch for.
simple.3.38: Just as smoke covers fire, dust covers a mirror and a womb covers a baby, desire covers our clear understanding in different degrees.
simple.3.39: Wisdom is covered by desire, the constant enemy of the wise, which is like a fire that is never satisfied no matter how much you feed it.
simple.3.40: Desire hides in the senses, the mind and the intellect, and works through them to cloud our judgment. Knowing where it lives helps us catch it.
simple.3.41: So begin by guiding your senses, and then overcome the desire that destroys knowledge and insight. Small daily discipline is where the change starts.
simple.3.42: The senses are powerful, the mind is higher than the senses, the intellect is higher than the mind, and the Self is higher still. You are more than your cravings.
simple.3.43: Knowing the Self to be beyond even the intellect, steady your lower self with your higher Self and overcome desire, though it is hard. It is possible, with patience.
simple.4.1: Krishna says this timeless teaching of yoga is very old: he first gave it to Vivasvan (the sun), who passed it to Manu, who passed it to King Ikshvaku. Wisdom has a long lineage.
simple.4.2: Wise kings handed this teaching down, one to the next, but over a long time it was lost. Even great wisdom fades unless each generation keeps it alive.
simple.4.3: Krishna now shares that same ancient teaching with Arjuna because Arjuna is his devoted friend. Deep truths are often passed on through trust and friendship.
simple.4.4: Arjuna is puzzled: Krishna was born recently, while the sun is ancient, so how could Krishna have taught it first? It is an honest, reasonable question.
simple.4.5: Krishna explains that both he and Arjuna have lived many lives; Krishna remembers them all, while Arjuna does not. Our view of our own story is limited.
simple.4.6: Krishna says that though he is unborn, unchanging and the Lord of all beings, he appears in the world by his own divine power. His coming is a free choice, not a compulsion.
simple.4.7: Whenever goodness declines and wrongdoing grows, Krishna says he appears in the world. It is a promise that the world is never abandoned.
simple.4.8: He comes, age after age, to protect the good, to end destructive wrongdoing, and to re-establish dharma (what is right). Goodness always gets renewed support.
simple.4.9: Whoever truly understands the divine nature of Krishna's birth and actions is not reborn after this life, but comes to him. Real understanding brings freedom.
simple.4.10: Many people, freed from clinging, fear and anger, focused on the Divine and taking refuge in it, have been purified by knowledge and reached the Divine. The path is well travelled.
simple.4.11: In whatever way people approach the Divine, the Divine meets them in that same way. Everyone, in their own way, is walking toward the same goal.
simple.4.12: People who want quick success in worldly life worship the gods (forces of nature), and such efforts bring fast results here. Krishna acknowledges this without judging it.
simple.4.13: Krishna says society's four kinds of roles were arranged according to people's qualities and the kind of work they do. Though he set this up, he himself remains unchanged and unattached.
simple.4.14: Actions do not stain Krishna, because he does not crave their results. Anyone who understands this is also freed from the bondage of action.
simple.4.15: Knowing this, seekers of freedom long ago kept doing their work. So Arjuna should act too, in the same spirit as the wise ones before him.
simple.4.16: What is action, and what is inaction? Even wise people get confused here. Krishna offers to explain it, because understanding it sets us free.
simple.4.17: We need to understand right action, wrong action and inaction, because the way action works is subtle. Thoughtfulness matters more than simple rules.
simple.4.18: The wise see stillness within activity and activity within stillness. They can be busy outside yet calm inside, and they notice that avoiding a duty is also a kind of action.
simple.4.19: When someone's efforts are free of selfish craving, and their actions are cleansed by wisdom, the wise call that person truly wise.
simple.4.20: Letting go of attachment to results, always content and not dependent on anything, such a person is not bound even while fully busy. Their inner freedom stays intact.
simple.4.21: Free from greed and grasping hopes, with a steady mind, doing only what the body needs, such a person does no wrong. Simple, uncraving action leaves no stain.
simple.4.22: Content with what comes naturally, beyond the push and pull of opposites, free from envy, and steady in success or failure, such a person acts without being bound.
simple.4.23: For someone free of clinging, with a mind settled in wisdom, who acts as an offering, their actions dissolve without leaving any binding trace.
simple.4.24: For one who sees the Divine everywhere, the offering, the act of offering, the fire and the one who offers are all Brahman (the Divine). Seeing this way, every action becomes sacred.
simple.4.25: Some offer worship to the gods, while others offer their very self into the Divine. Krishna starts to describe the many forms that yajna (offering) can take.
simple.4.26: Some offer their senses into the fire of self-restraint; others offer what they experience through the senses as an offering. Both control and mindful enjoyment can be sacred.
simple.4.27: Others offer all the work of the senses and the life-breath into the fire of self-control, lit by knowledge. Mastering ourselves can itself be an offering.
simple.4.28: Some offer wealth, some their discipline, some their practice of yoga, and some their study and learning. There are many ways to give.
simple.4.29: Some practice breath control, balancing the incoming and outgoing breath, as their offering. Even breathing, done with awareness, can be a spiritual practice.
simple.4.30: Others offer through moderate eating and care for their life-energy. All these people understand the spirit of offering, and it cleanses them.
simple.4.31: Those who enjoy what remains after offering taste something like nectar and reach the eternal. Without a spirit of giving, even this life does not go well, let alone the next.
simple.4.32: All these many kinds of offering are described in the scriptures, and all of them involve action. Understanding this sets you free.
simple.4.33: Offering wisdom is greater than offering material things, because all action finds its fulfilment in true understanding. Knowledge is where every effort leads.
simple.4.34: Learn this wisdom by approaching those who have realized the truth with humility, sincere questions and service. They will share it with you.
simple.4.35: Once you gain this wisdom, you will not be confused like this again, and you will see all beings in yourself and in the Divine. Everything becomes connected.
simple.4.36: Even if you have made more mistakes than anyone, the raft of wisdom can carry you across them all. No one is beyond the reach of understanding.
simple.4.37: Just as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge burns away the binding effects of past actions. Wisdom transforms our past.
simple.4.38: Nothing in the world purifies like true knowledge. Someone steady in yoga discovers it within themselves, naturally, in due time.
simple.4.39: A person with sincere faith, dedicated to the path and guiding their senses, gains this wisdom, and with it soon finds the deepest peace.
simple.4.40: Someone who refuses to learn, lacks trust and doubts everything finds no happiness, here or beyond. Endless doubt leaves no ground to stand on.
simple.4.41: One who has offered their actions through yoga, whose doubts are cleared by wisdom, and who is centered in the Self, is not bound by their actions.
simple.4.42: So, Krishna says, cut through the doubt in your heart with the sword of wisdom, take your stand in yoga, and rise up. Clarity leads to courageous action.
simple.5.1: Arjuna asks Krishna to settle it once and for all: is it better to give up action, or to act in the spirit of yoga? He wants one clear answer.
simple.5.2: Krishna says both giving up action and selfless action lead to the highest good, but acting selflessly is the better path for most people. Engagement beats withdrawal.
simple.5.3: A true renunciate is not someone who runs away from life, but someone who neither craves nor resents. Free from these push-and-pull opposites, they find freedom easily.
simple.5.4: Only beginners think wisdom and selfless action are completely different paths. The wise see that sincerely following one brings the fruit of both.
simple.5.5: The goal reached by the path of knowledge is also reached by the path of action. Seeing that they are really one is seeing clearly.
simple.5.6: Giving things up is hard without the practice of selfless action first. But someone who lives in harmony through yoga soon reaches the Divine.
simple.5.7: A person who acts selflessly, with a pure mind and guided senses, who sees the same Self in all beings, is not tainted by their actions, even while acting.
simple.5.8: Someone who knows the truth feels, 'I am not really the doer,' even while seeing, hearing, eating, walking, sleeping and breathing. They act without ego.
simple.5.9: Even while speaking, giving, taking, or blinking, they understand that it is simply the senses meeting their objects. This loosens ego's grip on everyday life.
simple.5.10: One who offers their actions to the Divine and lets go of clinging is untouched by wrongdoing, just as a lotus leaf sits in water but stays dry.
simple.5.11: People on the path of yoga use their body, mind, intellect and senses to act without clinging, for the sake of inner cleansing. Work becomes a way to grow.
simple.5.12: One who is steady and lets go of the fruits of action finds lasting peace, while one driven by desire and grasping at results gets tangled up. Letting go brings peace.
simple.5.13: A self-controlled person, inwardly letting go of all actions, rests happily in the body, the 'city of nine gates' (the body's openings), neither driven to act nor driving others.
simple.5.14: The Divine does not make people feel they are the doers, nor create their actions, nor tie actions to results; it is nature, our own inborn tendencies, that acts. The Divine is not pulling our strings.
simple.5.15: The Divine does not take on anyone's good or bad deeds. People get confused because their wisdom is covered by ignorance, like a cloud over the sun.
simple.5.16: But for those whose ignorance is cleared by knowing the Self, wisdom shines like the sun and reveals the highest truth. Understanding lights everything up.
simple.5.17: Those whose thoughts, hearts and goals rest wholly in the Divine have their mistakes washed away by wisdom and reach a state of no return to bondage.
simple.5.18: The wise see everyone with an equal eye, whether a learned and humble scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, or a person society looks down on. The same Self lives in all.
simple.5.19: Even in this life, those whose minds rest in equality have risen above the cycle of birth and death. The Divine is flawless and equal to all, and they rest in it.
simple.5.20: A person grounded in the Divine, with clear understanding, does not get overexcited by pleasant things or crushed by unpleasant ones. They stay steady.
simple.5.21: Not dependent on outside pleasures, such a person finds happiness within, and through connection with the Divine enjoys a joy that never ends.
simple.5.22: Pleasures from the senses have a beginning and an end, and so they also bring pain. The wise do not build their happiness on them.
simple.5.23: Whoever learns, in this very life, to withstand the surge of desire and anger is a true yogi and a truly happy person. Happiness grows from self-mastery.
simple.5.24: One whose happiness, joy and light come from within reaches complete freedom, becoming one with the Divine. Inner peace is the real treasure.
simple.5.25: Sages who have cleansed their faults, cleared their doubts, guided themselves, and care for the welfare of all beings reach complete freedom. Caring for all is part of the path.
simple.5.26: For those free from desire and anger, with calm minds and knowledge of the Self, freedom and peace surround them on every side, here and now.
simple.5.27: Krishna begins describing meditation: shutting out outside distractions, gently resting the gaze between the eyebrows, and balancing the in-breath and out-breath.
simple.5.28: With senses, mind and intellect gently guided, aiming for freedom, and free from desire, fear and anger, the meditator is truly free.
simple.5.29: Whoever knows Krishna as the one who receives all offerings and efforts, the Lord of all worlds, and the friend of every being, finds peace. The Divine is a friend, not a judge.
simple.6.1: Real spiritual life is not about dropping your responsibilities. Krishna says the true yogi does what needs doing without clinging to the rewards, unlike someone who simply gives up work or rituals.
simple.6.2: Renunciation and yoga are really the same thing: letting go of selfish wanting. You cannot find inner balance while your mind is busy chasing its own plans and cravings.
simple.6.3: When you are starting out, doing your work well is the path that trains you. Once you reach inner steadiness, calm and stillness help you stay there.
simple.6.4: You have reached yoga when you are no longer hooked by pleasures or by your actions and their results, and you have let go of the endless 'I want' plans in your head.
simple.6.5: You are the one who lifts yourself up. Your own mind can be your best friend or your worst enemy, so treat yourself as someone worth raising, not pulling down.
simple.6.6: When you have learned to guide your own mind, it becomes your ally. When it runs wild, it works against you as if it were an outside enemy.
simple.6.7: A person who has mastered themselves stays calm and settled whether it is hot or cold, pleasant or painful, and whether they are praised or insulted.
simple.6.8: Someone content with real understanding, and in charge of their senses, looks at a lump of clay, a stone and a bar of gold with the same calm eye. Things lose their power to unsettle them.
simple.6.9: The person who truly stands out holds the same goodwill toward everyone: friends, rivals, strangers, family, the kind and the unkind. A fair heart is a sign of real growth.
simple.6.10: To steady the mind, Krishna suggests regular time alone in a quiet place, with body and mind settled and free from restless craving and grasping.
simple.6.11: Meditation starts practically: find a clean, quiet spot and a steady seat, neither too high nor too low. In Krishna's time this meant layers of grass, skin and cloth.
simple.6.12: Sitting there, gather your attention to one point and let your thoughts and senses settle. The purpose of the practice is to clear and purify your inner life.
simple.6.13: Keep your body, head and neck upright and still, and let your gaze rest softly, as if toward the tip of your nose, instead of glancing around. A steady body helps a steady mind.
simple.6.14: Sit calm and unafraid, keeping a disciplined, self-restrained way of life (brahmacharya), with your mind gathered and resting on Krishna as your highest aim.
simple.6.15: Practicing this way again and again, with a balanced and gathered mind, the yogi reaches a deep peace that rests in Krishna and leads to freedom (liberation).
simple.6.16: Extremes get in the way. Meditation does not work well for someone who overeats or starves, or who oversleeps or hardly sleeps. The body needs care, not punishment.
simple.6.17: Moderation in food, play, work, sleep and waking is what lets yoga ease suffering. A balanced daily routine is itself a spiritual practice.
simple.6.18: A person is truly 'united' in yoga when their trained mind rests in the deeper Self and no longer craves the things of the senses.
simple.6.19: A well-trained mind is like a lamp in a place with no wind: its flame does not flicker. That steady, quiet glow is the picture of a mind settled in meditation.
simple.6.20: As practice calms the mind, it grows quiet, and you begin to see your true Self by your own inner light, finding contentment within instead of outside.
simple.6.21: In that state there is a deep joy beyond the senses, known by a clear and pure understanding. Once settled there, a person does not drift away from what is real.
simple.6.22: Having found this inner joy, you see no gain greater than it, and even heavy sorrow cannot shake you. It is a shelter that holds when life is hard.
simple.6.23: Yoga means unhooking from suffering. Krishna asks us to practice it with determination and without losing heart, even when progress seems slow.
simple.6.24: Let go of the cravings our imagination keeps cooking up, and use the mind to gently rein in the senses from every side.
simple.6.25: Go step by step. With patient, steady understanding, settle the mind in the Self and stop feeding other thoughts. Slow progress is still real progress.
simple.6.26: Whenever the restless mind wanders, for whatever reason, simply bring it back. This gentle returning, over and over, is the heart of meditation.
simple.6.27: Deep joy comes to the meditator whose mind is calm, whose passions have quieted, who is free from wrongdoing and becomes one with Brahman (the infinite reality).
simple.6.28: By practicing steadily like this, the yogi is cleansed of past wrongs and easily enjoys the boundless happiness of touching Brahman (the infinite reality).
simple.6.29: A mind made steady by yoga sees the same Self in every being, and every being in that Self. It looks on everyone with an equal, fair eye.
simple.6.30: Whoever sees Krishna everywhere, and everything in Krishna, is never lost to Krishna, and Krishna is never lost to them. It is a promise of a bond that does not break.
simple.6.31: A person rooted in this sense of oneness, who honors Krishna present in all beings, lives in Krishna, whatever their outer way of life looks like.
simple.6.32: The highest yogi feels others' joy and pain as their own, using their own heart as the measure. Compassion is a sign of real spiritual maturity.
simple.6.33: Arjuna is honest: this balanced state sounds wonderful, but his mind feels too restless to hold it steadily. It is a doubt almost everyone has felt.
simple.6.34: Arjuna calls the mind restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna does not scold him for saying so.
simple.6.35: Krishna agrees the mind is hard to control, but says it can be trained through two things: steady practice and letting go of attachment (detachment).
simple.6.36: Without self-discipline this yoga is hard to reach, but anyone who keeps trying with the right methods can get there.
simple.6.37: Arjuna asks a tender question: what happens to someone with sincere faith who tries, but whose mind slips off the path before reaching the goal?
simple.6.38: He worries such a person might lose both worldly success and spiritual progress, drifting like a broken cloud with nothing to hold on to.
simple.6.39: Arjuna asks Krishna to clear this doubt completely, trusting that no one else can answer it as well as he can.
simple.6.40: Krishna's answer is deeply reassuring: no one who does good ever comes to a bad end, in this world or the next. Sincere effort is never wasted.
simple.6.41: The one who strays from yoga first enjoys the worlds of good people for a long time, then is born into a pure and prosperous family where growth is easier.
simple.6.42: Or they may be born into a family of wise yogis, a rare and precious birth that gives them a strong start.
simple.6.43: There, the understanding they gained before comes back to them, and they strive even harder for the goal. Progress picks up where it left off.
simple.6.44: Their earlier practice carries them forward almost on its own. Even someone who simply wants to know yoga goes beyond mere ritual and book learning.
simple.6.45: By striving sincerely and being purified little by little over many lives, the yogi finally reaches the highest goal. Growth adds up over time.
simple.6.46: Krishna rates the yogi above those who only practice hardship, those who only study, and those who only perform rituals or works, and urges Arjuna to be a yogi.
simple.6.47: Of all yogis, Krishna holds dearest the one who, full of faith and with a heart absorbed in him, lovingly worships him. Devotion crowns the practice.
simple.7.1: Krishna promises to show Arjuna how to know him fully and without doubt: by keeping the mind lovingly connected to him, practicing yoga and relying on him.
simple.7.2: Krishna will share both knowledge (understanding) and realization (living experience of it). Once this is truly known, nothing essential is left to learn.
simple.7.3: Out of thousands of people, few truly seek the highest, and among those, few come to know Krishna as he really is. Real understanding is rare and precious, so it is worth sincere effort.
simple.7.4: Krishna describes his material nature as eightfold: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego (the sense of 'I'). Even our thoughts belong to this changing nature.
simple.7.5: Beyond this lower, material nature is Krishna's higher nature: the living spirit, the conscious life in every being, which holds the whole world up.
simple.7.6: These two natures, matter and spirit, are the source from which all beings come. Krishna is the origin of the whole universe and the place it returns to.
simple.7.7: Nothing is higher than Krishna. Everything is held together by him, the way pearls are held together by a thread you cannot see.
simple.7.8: Krishna points to the divine in everyday things: the taste of water, the light of the sun and moon, the sacred sound Om, sound in space, and human strength.
simple.7.9: He is the sweet smell of the earth, the brightness of fire, the life in every living thing, and the discipline of those who practice self-control.
simple.7.10: Krishna is the timeless seed of all beings, the intelligence in the wise and the brilliance in everything that shines. Every gift points back to its source.
simple.7.11: He is strength that is free from greed and attachment, and desire that is in harmony with dharma (what is right). Not all wanting is bad; wanting what is right is sacred.
simple.7.12: All qualities of life, whether calm and pure (sattva), active and passionate (rajas), or dull and heavy (tamas), come from Krishna. They exist in him, but he is not limited by them.
simple.7.13: Caught up in these three moods of nature, people do not recognize Krishna, who is beyond them and never changes. We mistake the passing show for the whole truth.
simple.7.14: Maya (the divine power of illusion), woven from these three qualities, is hard to see through on our own. But those who turn to Krishna can cross beyond it.
simple.7.15: When illusion clouds a person's understanding, they may drift into harmful ways and stop seeking the divine at all. Krishna is describing how confusion blocks the path.
simple.7.16: Four kinds of good people turn to Krishna: those in distress, those curious to understand, those seeking something they need, and the wise. Every sincere reason is honored.
simple.7.17: Of these, the wise person, always steady and devoted to the One, stands out. Krishna is very dear to them, and they are very dear to him.
simple.7.18: All four are noble, Krishna says, but the wise one is like his very own Self, because their mind rests in him as the highest goal.
simple.7.19: After many lifetimes, the wise person realizes 'Vasudeva (the divine) is everything' and comes to Krishna. Such a great soul is very rare.
simple.7.20: When desires pull our wisdom away, we turn to lesser powers and rituals, shaped by our own nature, hoping to get what we want.
simple.7.21: Whatever form of the divine a person sincerely worships, Krishna himself makes their faith steady. Sincere faith of any kind is supported by him.
simple.7.22: Worshipping that form with faith, they receive what they hoped for, but it is really Krishna who grants it.
simple.7.23: When we seek only limited things, the rewards are limited and do not last. Those who worship lesser powers reach them; those devoted to Krishna reach Krishna.
simple.7.24: People who do not understand think of the unmanifest divine as merely a limited, visible form, missing Krishna's higher nature, which is unchanging and supreme.
simple.7.25: Krishna is hidden from many by his yoga-maya (his veiling power). The confused world does not recognize him as unborn and imperishable.
simple.7.26: Krishna knows every being of the past, present and future, yet no one fully knows him. The divine is always greater than our grasp.
simple.7.27: From birth, every being is confused by pairs of opposites born of liking and disliking. Our likes and dislikes quietly shape how we see everything.
simple.7.28: But those who live rightly, whose wrongdoing has come to an end and who are freed from the pull of opposites, worship Krishna with firm resolve.
simple.7.29: Those who take refuge in Krishna while seeking freedom from aging and death come to understand Brahman (the infinite reality), the true Self and the whole nature of action.
simple.7.30: Those who know Krishna as present in the material world, in the divine powers and in all sacrifice keep their minds steady and know him even at the time of death.
simple.8.1: Arjuna asks Krishna to explain some big ideas: Brahman (the infinite reality), the individual self, karma (action), the material world and the divine powers. He wants to see the whole picture.
simple.8.2: He also asks who is the Lord of sacrifice dwelling within the body, and how people with a disciplined mind can know Krishna when life comes to its end.
simple.8.3: Krishna answers: Brahman is the imperishable Supreme; a being's essential nature is the Self; and karma is the creative action that brings beings into existence and sustains them.
simple.8.4: The physical world (adhibhuta) is what changes and passes away; the cosmic Person (Purusha) presides over the divine powers; and Krishna himself is the Lord of sacrifice (adhiyajna) living within every body.
simple.8.5: Whoever remembers Krishna as life comes to its close reaches his very being. Krishna says this with complete certainty, offering comfort rather than fear.
simple.8.6: Whatever we have thought about most during life tends to fill the mind at the end, and that shapes where we go next. Our everyday habits of thought matter.
simple.8.7: So Krishna says: remember me at all times, and do your work (fight your battle). Spiritual life is woven into daily duty, not separate from it.
simple.8.8: Through steady practice, a mind that does not wander off to other things, kept focused in meditation, reaches the Supreme, radiant Person.
simple.8.9: Krishna describes the one to meditate on: all-knowing, ancient, ruler of all, finer than an atom, supporter of everything, beyond imagining, shining like the sun beyond all darkness.
simple.8.10: A person who, at life's end, has a steady mind full of devotion, and through yoga gathers the life-breath (prana) between the eyebrows, reaches that radiant Supreme Person.
simple.8.11: Krishna now briefly describes the imperishable goal that the wise speak of, which the self-disciplined and passion-free enter, and for which people choose a life of restraint.
simple.8.12: He describes an advanced meditation: closing the 'gates' of the senses, holding the mind in the heart and drawing the life-breath upward to the head, fully absorbed in concentration.
simple.8.13: One who departs repeating Om, the one-syllable sound of Brahman, and remembering Krishna, reaches the highest goal.
simple.8.14: Krishna is easy to reach for someone who remembers him constantly, day after day, with a single-minded heart. Steady, everyday love is the key.
simple.8.15: The great souls who reach Krishna are not born again into this world of impermanence and pain; they have reached the highest fulfillment.
simple.8.16: Every realm, even the highest world of Brahma (the creator), is part of the cycle of coming and going. But reaching Krishna brings that cycle of rebirth to an end.
simple.8.17: Those who understand cosmic time know that one 'day' of Brahma lasts a thousand ages, and his 'night' is just as long. Our timescales are tiny next to the universe's.
simple.8.18: At the dawn of that cosmic day, all things emerge from the Unmanifest (the unseen source); when night falls, they dissolve back into it.
simple.8.19: The same multitude of beings comes forth again and again, dissolving at nightfall and re-emerging at dawn, carried along by the great cycle.
simple.8.20: But beyond this unseen source there is another, eternal Unmanifest that is never destroyed, even when all beings dissolve.
simple.8.21: This imperishable, unmanifest reality is the highest goal. Those who reach it do not return; it is Krishna's supreme home.
simple.8.22: That Supreme Person, in whom all beings live and who fills everything, is reached through wholehearted devotion. Love is the way.
simple.8.23: Krishna now explains the times of passing after which yogis either return to this world or do not. He presents them calmly, as paths to understand.
simple.8.24: Those who know Brahman and depart along the path of fire, light, day, the bright half of the moon and the sun's northern course reach Brahman. Many teachers read this light as a symbol of wisdom.
simple.8.25: Those who depart along the path of smoke, night, the dark half of the moon and the sun's southern course reach the light of the moon and then return to be born again.
simple.8.26: These two paths, the bright and the dark, have always existed: one leads to no return, the other leads back again.
simple.8.27: A yogi who understands these paths is not confused by them. So Krishna's real advice is simple: stay steady in yoga at all times.
simple.8.28: The yogi who understands this goes beyond all the merit gained from study, ritual, self-discipline and charity, and reaches the supreme, original home.
simple.9.1: Krishna offers Arjuna his deepest teaching because Arjuna listens with an open, non-cynical heart. Real knowledge here means understanding you actually live, not just facts, and it frees you from what weighs you down.
simple.9.2: Krishna calls this the 'royal' knowledge: the most valuable and purifying of all. It can be experienced directly, fits with living rightly, is joyful and easy to practise, and its benefit never fades.
simple.9.3: Without trust in this way of living, people keep going round the same cycles of life without reaching what they truly long for. Faith here means a willingness to try the path, not blind belief.
simple.9.4: Krishna says his unseen presence fills the whole universe. Everything rests in him, yet he is not limited or contained by any single thing, the way space holds everything without being trapped by it.
simple.9.5: This is a gentle riddle: the Divine holds up all beings yet is untouched by them. Krishna calls it his mystery. It points to a presence that supports everything without being caught up in it.
simple.9.6: Like the wind that blows everywhere yet always moves within the sky, all beings move within the Divine. However far we roam, we never fall outside that larger space.
simple.9.7: At the end of each great cosmic age, all beings return into nature's resting state, and at the start of the next they are sent forth again. Life moves in vast rhythms of rest and renewal.
simple.9.8: Krishna, working through nature, brings the many beings into existence again and again. Beings follow nature's patterns, which reminds us how much of life runs by forces bigger than our personal control.
simple.9.9: Though Krishna sets the whole universe in motion, these actions do not bind him, because he is unattached, like a calm witness. Acting fully without clinging is the model for us too.
simple.9.10: Nature does the work of producing all moving and still things, under Krishna's gentle oversight. That is how the world keeps turning: an order holds even the busiest, most chaotic movement.
simple.9.11: When the Divine appears in an ordinary human form, people who look only at the surface miss it. It is a reminder that the sacred can hide in the plain and familiar.
simple.9.12: When people live from ego and confusion, their hopes, efforts and learning end up empty. Without a deeper aim, even busy lives can feel like they are going nowhere.
simple.9.13: Great-hearted people, drawing on the divine qualities within them, turn wholeheartedly to Krishna, recognizing him as the unchanging source of all life. Their devotion flows from understanding, not obligation.
simple.9.14: These devoted people keep the Divine close through song and praise, steady effort, firm commitments and humble bowing. Their love is expressed in daily, practical ways.
simple.9.15: Others honour the Divine through the path of knowledge: seeing God as one, as distinct, or as present in countless forms. There is more than one sincere way to approach the sacred.
simple.9.16: Krishna names himself as every part of a sacred ritual: the rite, the offering, the herbs, the chant, the butter, the fire, the act of offering. The holy is the whole of the act, not just its target.
simple.9.17: Krishna describes himself as father, mother, grandparent and supporter of the world, the one thing truly worth knowing, the purifier, the sound Om and the sacred texts. He is family and wisdom at once.
simple.9.18: This lovely list names the Divine as goal, support, master, witness, home, shelter and friend; as beginning, end and resting place; as the treasure and the seed that never dies. Every need of the heart finds a home here.
simple.9.19: Sun's heat, rain held and released, life and death, being and not-being: Krishna says all of it comes from him. Even life's opposites belong to one larger whole.
simple.9.20: People who perform rituals to win heaven's pleasures do get them. The verse is not against such rewards; it simply sets up a contrast with something more lasting.
simple.9.21: Heavenly rewards run out like money spent, and then people return to ordinary life to start again. Chasing rewards keeps us coming and going without lasting peace.
simple.9.22: For those who keep the Divine in mind with steady love, Krishna promises to bring what they lack and protect what they have. It is a promise of care, not of wealth.
simple.9.23: Even people who sincerely worship other deities are really reaching toward Krishna, he says, though not in the fullest way. Sincere faith in any form is honoured.
simple.9.24: The Divine is the true receiver of every sincere offering. When people do not see this, their worship stays tied to short-term gains, and they keep cycling back into ordinary life.
simple.9.25: We become like what we devote ourselves to. Those who worship gods, ancestors or spirits reach those, and those who love Krishna come to Krishna. Our deepest focus shapes where we end up.
simple.9.26: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: Krishna gladly accepts the simplest gift offered with love. What matters is the heart behind the gift, not its size or cost.
simple.9.27: Whatever you do, eat, give or strive for, Krishna invites you to do it as an offering. Ordinary daily life can itself become a way of love.
simple.9.28: When every action is offered rather than grasped for personal gain, you are freed from being tied to its good or bad results. Letting go this way brings inner freedom and closeness to the Divine.
simple.9.29: Krishna is equally present to all beings; he plays no favourites and hates no one. Yet those who turn to him in love feel that closeness, and he lives in them as they live in him.
simple.9.30: Even someone who has done very wrong, if they turn to Krishna with full devotion, should be seen as good, because they have made the right decision. A sincere turning point counts more than the past.
simple.9.31: Such a person quickly becomes good and finds lasting peace. Krishna asks Arjuna to announce boldly: anyone who loves the Divine is never lost.
simple.9.32: Krishna insists that anyone who takes refuge in him, whatever their birth, gender, work or social standing, reaches the highest goal. In his time this was a radical welcome to all.
simple.9.33: If even those whom society looked down on reach the goal, so can anyone. Since this world is passing and full of difficulty, Krishna urges turning toward what is lasting.
simple.9.34: Krishna sums up the path: keep your mind on me, love me, offer to me, bow to me. When your whole self is turned toward the Divine, you come home to it.
simple.10.1: Krishna speaks again to Arjuna, calling him dear and saying he shares this for Arjuna's good. Real teaching comes from care for the listener.
simple.10.2: Not even gods or great sages fully know where Krishna comes from, because he is the source of them all. The deepest reality is bigger than any mind that tries to grasp it.
simple.10.3: Whoever understands the Divine as unborn, without beginning, and Lord of all worlds sees clearly and is freed from wrongdoing. Knowing the true source changes how we live.
simple.10.4: Krishna begins a list of human qualities: understanding, wisdom, clear thinking, forgiveness, truthfulness, self-control, calm, joy and sorrow, birth and death, fear and courage. All of our inner life has one source.
simple.10.5: The list continues: non-violence, balance, contentment, discipline, generosity, fame and disgrace. All these varied states of beings arise from Krishna. Even our inner states are part of a larger whole.
simple.10.6: The great sages and ancient founders of humanity, Krishna says, were born from his mind, and all beings descend from them. Every generation traces back to one source.
simple.10.7: Whoever truly grasps Krishna's many expressions and his power becomes steady and unshakeable in spirit. Seeing the Divine behind the world brings deep stability.
simple.10.8: Krishna says he is the source of everything and all things come forth from him. Wise people who understand this turn to him with heartfelt love.
simple.10.9: Those whose thoughts and lives are centred on the Divine love to talk about it with one another, sharing insights and finding joy and contentment together. Spiritual friendship lifts everyone.
simple.10.10: To those who stay devoted with love, Krishna gives clear understanding (inner wisdom to see what matters), which guides them to him. Love opens the way to wisdom.
simple.10.11: Out of pure compassion, Krishna, living within each heart, lights a lamp of knowledge that removes the darkness of ignorance. Inner clarity is a gift of grace.
simple.10.12: Arjuna responds with wonder, naming Krishna as the highest reality, the supreme home, the purifier, eternal, divine, the first God, unborn and everywhere.
simple.10.13: Arjuna notes that great sages like Narada, Asita, Devala and Vyasa have all said this, and now Krishna himself confirms it. Tradition and personal experience meet.
simple.10.14: Arjuna says he accepts everything Krishna has told him as true, and admits that neither gods nor demons fully understand Krishna's nature. It is humble, trusting acceptance.
simple.10.15: Only Krishna truly knows himself, Arjuna says, calling him source of all beings, God of gods and Lord of the world. The infinite can only be fully known from within.
simple.10.16: Arjuna asks Krishna to describe fully the divine glories through which he fills all worlds. He wants to see how the Divine shows up in everything.
simple.10.17: Arjuna asks a practical question: how can I keep you in mind, and in which things should I think of you? He wants a way to remember the sacred in daily life.
simple.10.18: Arjuna asks to hear again, in detail, about Krishna's power and glory, saying he can never get enough of these life-giving words. True wisdom never feels like too much.
simple.10.19: Krishna agrees to name his most prominent glories, but says there is no end to them in detail. The list that follows is a sample, not a complete catalogue.
simple.10.20: Krishna first says he is the Self living in the heart of every being, and their beginning, middle and end. Before any outward glory, the sacred lives within everyone.
simple.10.21: Among bright and powerful things Krishna names the best: Vishnu among the sun gods, the sun among lights, the moon among stars. Wherever you see radiance, think of the Divine.
simple.10.22: Krishna is the musical Sama Veda, the king of the gods, the mind among the senses and consciousness in living beings. Awareness itself points to the sacred.
simple.10.23: Among powerful beings Krishna names Shiva, Kubera the lord of wealth, fire, and Mount Meru. The greatest in each group points beyond itself to the Divine.
simple.10.24: Krishna is Brihaspati, chief of priests, Skanda, chief of generals, and the ocean among waters. In leadership, strength and vastness, we can glimpse the sacred.
simple.10.25: Krishna is Bhrigu among sages, Om among sounds, quiet repetition of a sacred word among offerings, and the Himalayas among mountains. Stillness and steadiness reveal the Divine.
simple.10.26: Krishna is the sacred peepul (fig) tree, the sage Narada, the celestial musician Chitraratha and the sage Kapila. Wisdom, music and the living tree all carry his presence.
simple.10.27: Among horses and elephants Krishna names the legendary royal ones, and among people, the king. Excellence and noble leadership point to the sacred.
simple.10.28: Krishna is the thunderbolt among weapons, the wish-fulfilling cow, the power of love that brings new life, and the serpent king Vasuki. Power used for life reflects the Divine.
simple.10.29: Krishna names himself as the great serpent Ananta, Varuna lord of waters, the chief of ancestors, and Yama who keeps order. Even guardians of justice and endings reflect him.
simple.10.30: Krishna is Prahlada, the devoted boy born among demons; time among all that measures; the lion among animals; and Garuda among birds. Goodness can shine even in unlikely places.
simple.10.31: Krishna is the wind that purifies, Rama among warriors, the mightiest of sea creatures and the river Ganga. Cleansing, courage and life-giving flow all reflect him.
simple.10.32: Krishna is the beginning, middle and end of all creation, the knowledge of the Self among sciences, and honest reasoning in debate. The search for truth itself is sacred.
simple.10.33: Krishna is the first letter 'A', the simplest joining of words, endless time and the one who gives each action its result. He is in the building blocks of language and life.
simple.10.34: Krishna is death that takes all and the source of everything yet to be born. He also names qualities like fame, beauty, speech, memory, intelligence, steadiness and patience.
simple.10.35: Krishna is the finest hymn, the Gayatri rhythm, the best month and spring, the season of flowers. Beauty and freshness in time and nature carry the Divine.
simple.10.36: Krishna is even the cleverness of the gambler, the brilliance of the brilliant, victory, determination and the goodness of good people. Every kind of ability draws on one source, so the call is to use it well.
simple.10.37: Krishna names himself among his own family, among the Pandavas as Arjuna himself, among sages as Vyasa, and among poets as Ushana. Arjuna learns he too reflects the Divine.
simple.10.38: Krishna is the authority that keeps order, wise strategy in those who seek success, silence among secrets and wisdom in the wise. Quiet, wise strength reflects him.
simple.10.39: Krishna says he is the seed of all beings; nothing, moving or still, could exist without him. He is the root of everything that lives.
simple.10.40: There is no end to Krishna's divine glories; what he has shared is only a small sample. The sacred is endless, always more than we can list.
simple.10.41: Wherever you find anything glorious, beautiful or powerful, know that it springs from a spark of Krishna's splendour. This is the key to the whole chapter.
simple.10.42: Krishna ends: why worry over all these details? With just one small part of himself he supports the entire universe. The point is not the list, but the awe it awakens.
simple.11.1: Arjuna says Krishna's teaching, given out of kindness, has cleared away his confusion. Hearing truth spoken with care can lift a heavy fog from the mind.
simple.11.2: Arjuna has heard how beings come and go, and about Krishna's endless greatness. Understanding has grown, and now a deeper longing stirs.
simple.11.3: Having heard Krishna describe himself, Arjuna now longs to actually see his divine form. He wants experience, not only explanation.
simple.11.4: Arjuna asks humbly: if you think I am able to see it, please show me. He does not demand; he leaves it to Krishna's judgement. Humble asking is the right way to seek.
simple.11.5: Krishna invites Arjuna to look: see my forms by the hundreds and thousands, in countless colours and shapes. The Divine is overflowing variety, not one narrow image.
simple.11.6: Krishna shows the many gods of the sky, light, storm and healing, and wonders never seen before. The sacred contains more than we have ever imagined.
simple.11.7: Krishna invites Arjuna to see the whole universe, moving and still, gathered in one place in his body. Everything belongs to one great whole.
simple.11.8: Krishna explains that ordinary eyes cannot see this, so he gives Arjuna a 'divine eye', a new way of seeing. Some truths need a changed perspective, not just sharper sight.
simple.11.9: Sanjaya, the narrator, tells the blind king that Krishna, master of yoga, then revealed his supreme cosmic form to Arjuna. The great vision begins.
simple.11.10: The form has countless mouths and eyes, wonders, ornaments and raised weapons. It is a picture of a reality that sees everything, holds everything and acts everywhere.
simple.11.11: The cosmic form wears heavenly garlands, robes and fragrances, shining and endless, with faces on every side. It is awe-inspiring beauty with no edges.
simple.11.12: If a thousand suns blazed in the sky at once, that might hint at the brilliance of this form. It is a way of saying: far beyond anything we can picture.
simple.11.13: Arjuna sees the whole universe, with all its many parts, resting together in the body of the God of gods. Unity holds all diversity.
simple.11.14: Filled with wonder, his hair standing on end, Arjuna bows his head and joins his palms. Awe naturally leads to reverence and humility.
simple.11.15: Arjuna describes what he sees: all the gods, all kinds of beings, Brahma the creator on his lotus, sages and celestial serpents, all within Krishna. Everything sacred is gathered in one.
simple.11.16: Arjuna sees endless arms, faces and eyes in every direction, with no beginning, middle or end. The infinite cannot be measured or bordered.
simple.11.17: Krishna's form shines like fire and sun, so bright it is hard to look at, yet Arjuna recognizes crown, mace and discus. Even overwhelming glory has a familiar face.
simple.11.18: Arjuna recognizes Krishna as the imperishable, the one supreme thing to know, the resting place of the universe and the protector of eternal goodness (dharma, the right order of life).
simple.11.19: Arjuna sees a form without beginning or end, endlessly powerful, with sun and moon for eyes and fire for a mouth, warming the whole universe. Nature itself becomes the face of the Divine.
simple.11.20: The form fills all space between earth and sky, and the worlds tremble at its wonder and power. This is awe: being shaken by something far greater than ourselves.
simple.11.21: Hosts of gods enter into Krishna, some praying with folded hands, while sages and perfected beings sing his praises. All of creation responds to the vision with reverence.
simple.11.22: All the heavenly beings, gods, spirits, singers and sages, gaze at the form in amazement. Even the greatest beings feel wonder before the infinite.
simple.11.23: Seeing the vast form with countless mouths, eyes, limbs and fearsome teeth, the worlds are shaken, and so is Arjuna. He honestly admits how overwhelmed he feels.
simple.11.24: The form touches the sky, blazes with colour, with wide mouths and fiery eyes. Arjuna says he has lost his courage and peace. Meeting the infinite can unsettle our usual sense of control.
simple.11.25: Faced with mouths blazing like the fire at the end of time, Arjuna loses his bearings and asks for mercy. Being honest about feeling small, and asking for grace, is a humble response.
simple.11.26: Arjuna sees the warriors of both armies, including great elders like Bhishma, Drona and Karna, being drawn into the form. Time gathers in even the mightiest.
simple.11.27: This vivid image shows the warriors rushing into the form's mouths. It is a symbolic picture of time and change, showing that no one, however mighty, stays forever.
simple.11.28: Just as rivers rush toward the ocean, the heroes of the world flow into the blazing form. Every life flows on toward its natural end, as surely as rivers reach the sea.
simple.11.29: As moths fly into a flame, beings rush toward their end. The image invites us to see how swiftly life moves and to live wisely within it.
simple.11.30: The form draws in all worlds on every side, its brilliance filling the universe. It is the image of time drawing everything into itself, calmly and completely.
simple.11.31: Arjuna asks: who are you, in this awesome form? He bows, asks for mercy and wants to understand. Even overwhelmed, he keeps seeking to know.
simple.11.32: Krishna answers: I am Time, the great force that brings all things to their end. These warriors' fates are already moving toward completion, with or without you.
simple.11.33: So rise and do your part, Krishna says; the outcome is already in larger hands. Be simply an instrument. We are invited to act fully without carrying the burden of controlling everything.
simple.11.34: Krishna names the great warriors and says their end is already set; Arjuna need not be crushed by fear. He should do his duty with courage.
simple.11.35: Hearing this, Arjuna trembles, folds his hands, bows low and speaks with a choked voice. He is deeply moved, and this awe becomes humble surrender.
simple.11.36: Arjuna says it is right that the world rejoices in praising Krishna, that harmful forces flee and the wise bow to him. Goodness naturally responds to the Divine with joy.
simple.11.37: Arjuna asks: why would they not bow? You are greater than the creator himself, infinite, Lord of gods, home of the universe, beyond what is and what is not.
simple.11.38: Arjuna calls Krishna the first God, the ancient being, the final refuge of the universe, both the knower and what is known, filling everything with infinite forms.
simple.11.39: Arjuna sees the gods of wind, death, fire, water, moon and creation all as Krishna, and bows again and again, a thousand times. Every power of nature points to one source.
simple.11.40: Arjuna bows in front, behind and on every side, because Krishna is everywhere and is everything. Reverence that has no direction left out.
simple.11.41: Arjuna remembers calling Krishna 'my friend' casually, not knowing his greatness, from carelessness or affection. Seeing someone's true depth can make us rethink how we have treated them.
simple.11.42: He asks forgiveness for any disrespect in joking, playing, resting or eating together, alone or in company. Familiarity can make us careless, and owning it is a gift to the relationship.
simple.11.43: Arjuna calls Krishna the father of the world, worthy of honour, the greatest teacher, with none equal to him. Respect grows as understanding grows.
simple.11.44: Bowing low, Arjuna asks for forgiveness as a father forgives a son, a friend a friend, a lover the beloved. He trusts in forgiveness rooted in love.
simple.11.45: Arjuna is thrilled at what he has seen, yet his mind is shaken. He asks to see Krishna's gentle form again. Awe and comfort both have their place.
simple.11.46: Arjuna asks to see Krishna in his familiar, four-armed form, crowned and holding mace and discus. After the infinite, he longs for the personal and approachable.
simple.11.47: Krishna says, with grace, he has shown this radiant, ancient, infinite form, seen by no one else before Arjuna. The vision was a gift, not something earned.
simple.11.48: Neither study, charity, ritual nor harsh discipline can win this vision, Krishna says; it was given to Arjuna alone. Grace is beyond what effort alone can achieve.
simple.11.49: Krishna comforts Arjuna: do not be afraid or confused by this mighty form. Be at peace, with a glad heart, and see my familiar form again. The Divine reassures.
simple.11.50: Sanjaya says Krishna returned to his own gentle form and comforted the shaken Arjuna. The infinite is also tender and kind.
simple.11.51: Seeing Krishna's gentle human form again, Arjuna feels calm and himself again. Familiar love restores our balance after something overwhelming.
simple.11.52: Krishna says the form Arjuna has seen is extremely rare; even the gods long to see it. Arjuna should value what he has been given.
simple.11.53: Krishna repeats that study, discipline, giving or ritual alone cannot win this vision. Something more personal is needed.
simple.11.54: That 'something more' is wholehearted, single-minded devotion. Through love, Krishna says, he can truly be known, seen and united with.
