4-4.teaching: Even wise people find it hard to know what true action and inaction are. Krishna says the wise can be calm inside while busy outside. When we let go of attachment to results and stay content, our work no longer weighs on us.
4-4.keyIdea: Be fully busy, and still be at rest inside.

apply.scenario: You are a new parent juggling work and a baby. You feel you can only find peace once life slows down, months or years from now.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Put peace on hold; it is only possible once life is quieter.
Cut back on caring for the baby so you can relax more.
Stay engaged in your duties while letting go of clinging, so peace is found within the busyness.
Push yourself harder to finish everything so you can rest later.
apply.why: In 4.18 Krishna says the wise see inaction in action, and in 4.20 that one who is content and unattached is free even while fully engaged.

4-4.reflect: What would it feel like to be at peace in the middle of my busiest day?
4-4.practice: During one busy task today, pause for one breath and notice the stillness under the activity.

4-5.title: Steady in success and failure
4-5.teaching: A person who is content with what comes, free of envy and even-minded in success and failure, can act without being bound. When work is done as an offering, it leaves no heavy trace. Seen this way, everything, even everyday tasks, becomes sacred.
4-5.keyIdea: Win or lose, keep your center.

apply.scenario: A colleague got the promotion you wanted. You feel envious and keep comparing your achievements to theirs all week.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Look for flaws in their work to prove you deserved it more.
Pretend you are fine while quietly resenting them.
Decide never to try for promotions again so you do not get hurt.
Notice the envy, let it go, and stay steady in your own work whether you win or lose.
apply.why: In 4.22 Krishna describes the free person as content, free from envy, and even-minded in success and failure.

4-5.reflect: How might my week feel if my peace did not depend on how I compare to others?
4-5.practice: Congratulate someone sincerely today on a success you wish had been yours.

4-6.title: Many ways to give
4-6.teaching: Krishna describes many kinds of yajna (offering): giving wealth, practicing self-discipline, studying, eating moderately, even breathing with awareness. There is no single right way to give. When life becomes an offering, it gains a deep sweetness.
4-6.keyIdea: Any part of life can become an offering.

apply.scenario: You want to contribute to your community, but you have little money to donate and feel you have nothing worthwhile to give.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Wait until you earn more, since money is the only real way to give.
Offer what you do have, like time, skills or care, since there are many ways to give.
Feel guilty and stay away from community events for now.
Give only when someone directly asks you for help.
apply.why: In 4.28 Krishna says some offer wealth, some discipline and some study, showing that offerings take many forms.

4-6.reflect: What do I have, besides money, that I could offer to others?
4-6.practice: Offer one skill or one hour of your time to someone who could use it this week.

4-7.title: Learn humbly, see the whole
4-7.teaching: The offering of wisdom is greater than offering things, because all action finds its fulfilment in understanding. Krishna says to learn from those who know, with humility, questions and service. This wisdom helps us see all beings as connected, and no past mistake is beyond its reach.
4-7.keyIdea: Humble questions open the door to wisdom.

apply.scenario: You have just joined a new team. A senior colleague knows a lot, but asking feels embarrassing, so you keep struggling silently on your own.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Keep struggling alone so no one thinks you are weak.
Pretend you already know and figure it out later.
Approach them humbly, ask sincere questions, and offer help where you can.
Wait for them to notice you are struggling and offer help first.
apply.why: In 4.34 Krishna says to learn from the wise through humility, sincere questions and service.

4-7.reflect: What am I too proud or shy to ask about, and who could help me learn it?
4-7.practice: Ask one sincere question today to someone who knows more than you about something.

4-8.title: Cut through doubt and rise
4-8.teaching: Nothing purifies like real understanding, and it grows through sincere trust and steady practice. Endless doubt leaves us stuck and unhappy. Krishna urges Arjuna to cut through the doubt in his heart with wisdom and rise to act.
4-8.keyIdea: Let wisdom cut through doubt, then stand up and act.

apply.scenario: You have wanted to start learning music for years, but you keep doubting whether you are talented enough, so you never begin.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Look honestly at the doubt, trust the path, and take the first step today.
Wait until you are completely sure you will be good at it.
Ask everyone you know if they think you have talent first.
Give up the idea, since doubt means it is not meant for you.
apply.why: In 4.42 Krishna tells Arjuna to cut through doubt with the sword of wisdom and rise, and 4.40 notes constant doubt brings no happiness.

4-8.reflect: Which doubt has been holding me back the longest, and is it really true?
4-8.practice: Take one small first step today on something you have been doubting yourself about.

5-1.title: Engage, don't escape
5-1.teaching: Arjuna asks whether giving up action or acting selflessly is better. Krishna says both lead to the goal, but selfless action is the better path. A true renunciate is not someone who quits life, but someone free from craving and resentment.
5-1.keyIdea: Real renunciation happens in the heart, not by walking away.

apply.scenario: Your sports team is full of drama and petty arguments. You are thinking about quitting the game you love just to escape all the noise.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Quit immediately; walking away is the purest way to find peace.
Stay but complain about everyone so they know how you feel.
Keep playing and doing your part, while letting go of craving and resentment toward the drama.
Take sides in the arguments so at least you are on the winning side.
apply.why: In 5.2 Krishna says selfless action is better than giving up action, and 5.3 says a true renunciate neither craves nor resents.

5-1.reflect: Am I trying to escape something outside me, when what needs to change is inside?
5-1.practice: Notice one resentment today and let it go for just one hour, while still showing up.

5-2.title: Like a lotus in water
5-2.teaching: Krishna says the one who acts while letting go of clinging is like a lotus leaf: it sits in water but stays dry. Such a person sees, hears, eats and works without ego taking over. They live fully in the world without being stained by it.
5-2.keyIdea: Be in the world without being soaked by it.

apply.scenario: You work in a very competitive office where gossip and backstabbing are common. You worry that just being there will turn you into that kind of person.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Join the gossip so you are not left out or targeted.
Do your work fully and kindly, staying untouched by the negativity, like a lotus in water.
Quit right away, since no one can stay good in that environment.
Stay silent and cold with everyone so no one can affect you.
apply.why: In 5.10 Krishna says one who acts without clinging is untouched by wrongdoing, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.

5-2.reflect: In which environment do I most need to be like a lotus leaf, present but unstained?
5-2.practice: Next time you hear gossip, gently change the subject or simply do not add to it.

5-3.title: Peace comes from letting go
5-3.teaching: People on the path of yoga use their whole selves, body, mind and senses, to act without clinging, as a way to grow. The one who lets go of the results finds lasting peace; the one driven by grasping gets tangled. The Divine does not force our choices; our own nature shapes what we do.
5-3.keyIdea: Grasping tangles; letting go brings peace.

apply.scenario: You have spent months caring for an elderly parent. You keep hoping they will finally say how grateful they are, and feel hurt each day they do not.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Tell them directly that they owe you thanks for all your effort.
Care for them less until they show they appreciate you.
Hand over all caregiving to a sibling since it is not rewarding.
Keep caring with love, letting go of the need for a particular response.
apply.why: In 5.12 Krishna says the steady person who lets go of the fruit of action finds lasting peace, while grasping at results binds.

5-3.reflect: What reward am I quietly waiting for, and how would it feel to set it down?
5-3.practice: Do one caring act today and consciously let go of any thanks it might bring.

5-4.title: See everyone with equal eyes
5-4.teaching: When wisdom clears away confusion, it lights up everything like the sun. The wise see the same Self in a scholar, an animal, or a person society looks down on. Seeing everyone with an equal eye is a sign of real understanding.
5-4.keyIdea: The same light shines in everyone.

apply.scenario: At a party, you notice yourself being warm to the important guests but barely glancing at the staff serving food and cleaning up.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Treat everyone, guests and staff alike, with the same warmth and respect.
Focus on the important guests, since they matter more for your future.
Be polite to staff only when others are watching.
Avoid everyone so you do not have to choose.
apply.why: In 5.18 Krishna says the wise look with an equal eye on a learned person, animals, and someone society looks down on.

5-4.reflect: Whom do I tend to overlook, and what might I see if I looked at them with equal eyes?
5-4.practice: Learn the name of someone you see often but have never really noticed, and thank them.

5-5.title: Joy that comes from within
5-5.teaching: Pleasures from outside things begin and end, so they cannot give lasting happiness. A person who learns, in this life, to withstand the surge of desire and anger finds a deeper joy within. That inner light is a happiness no one can take away.
5-5.keyIdea: Outer pleasures fade; inner joy lasts.

apply.scenario: You just bought the new phone you wanted for months. A week later the excitement is gone and you are already eyeing the next upgrade.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Buy the next upgrade quickly to bring the excitement back.
Feel bad about yourself for buying the phone in the first place.
Notice that sense pleasures come and go, and seek steadier joy within.
Save up for something even bigger that will surely satisfy you.
apply.why: In 5.22 Krishna says pleasures from contact have a beginning and an end, so the wise do not build their happiness on them.

5-5.reflect: What brings me a quiet joy that does not depend on buying or getting anything?
5-5.practice: Spend ten minutes today doing something that brings joy without spending money.

5-6.title: Rest in the friend of all
5-6.teaching: The wise who care for the welfare of all beings and let go of desire and anger find freedom all around them. Krishna describes a calm meditation that steadies the senses and breath. He ends by naming himself the friend of all beings, and knowing this brings peace.
5-6.keyIdea: Peace grows when you know you are befriended.

apply.scenario: You are grieving the loss of a close friend. You feel alone, restless and angry at the world, and cannot sit still or sleep well.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Keep busy every minute so you never have to feel the grief.
Take quiet moments to steady your breath, and remember you are held by a friend to all beings.
Push away anyone who tries to comfort you until the anger passes.
Tell yourself grief is weakness and force yourself to move on.
apply.why: In 5.27 to 5.28 Krishna describes calming the senses and breath, and 5.29 says knowing him as the friend of all beings brings peace.

5-6.reflect: What would change if I truly felt the Divine as my friend rather than my judge?
5-6.practice: Sit for three minutes today, breathe evenly, and silently say: 'I am not alone.'

6-1.title: Be your own best friend
6-1.teaching: Spiritual life is not about escaping your duties; it is doing what needs doing without clinging to rewards. No one else can lift you up for you. Your own mind can become your best friend or your harshest enemy, and you get to choose which.
6-1.keyIdea: Your own mind can be your best friend or your worst enemy.

apply.scenario: You failed an important exam, and your inner voice keeps saying 'you're hopeless, why bother?' A friend suggests you just drop the course.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Drop the course quietly so you never have to feel this bad again.
Wait for a teacher or parent to step in and tell you what to do next.
Speak to yourself like a good friend would: admit the setback, then make a small plan to lift yourself up.
Keep replaying the failure until you feel bad enough to finally change.
apply.why: In 6.5 Krishna says we should raise ourselves by our own effort and never drag ourselves down, because the self can be our friend or our enemy.

6-1.reflect: When things go wrong, does your inner voice sound more like a friend or a critic?
6-1.practice: Notice one harsh thought about yourself today and rewrite it the way a kind friend would say it.

6-2.title: Stay steady through praise and blame
6-2.teaching: When you learn to guide your mind, it becomes your ally. A settled person stays balanced in heat or cold, pleasure or pain, honor or insult, and offers the same goodwill to everyone. Quiet time alone helps build this steadiness.
6-2.keyIdea: Stay the same person whether you are praised or criticized.

apply.scenario: On Monday your manager praised you in a meeting; on Thursday she criticized your report in front of the team. You feel like a hero one day and a failure the next.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Take the feedback calmly, learn what is useful, and let neither the praise nor the criticism define you.
Bring up Monday's praise to remind everyone that you are actually good at this.
Stop sharing your work in meetings so you can't be criticized in public again.
Decide your manager dislikes you and stay cool and distant with her from now on.
apply.why: In 6.7 Krishna describes the self-mastered person as balanced in pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor.

6-2.reflect: Whose approval moves your mood the most, and what would it feel like to depend on it a little less?
6-2.practice: Spend five quiet minutes alone today, phone away, simply noticing your breath.

6-3.title: Set up a simple meditation habit
6-3.teaching: Krishna gives down-to-earth instructions for meditation: a clean, quiet spot, a steady seat, an upright body and a gathered mind. He also warns against extremes. Eating or sleeping too much or too little makes practice harder, not holier.
6-3.keyIdea: A clean spot, a steady seat, an upright spine, a gathered mind.

apply.scenario: You want to start meditating. A friend says the 'serious' way is to skip meals and cut your sleep to four hours so your mind gets sharper.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Follow your friend's plan, since harder must mean more spiritual.
Meditate lying in bed with your phone nearby so it feels relaxed and easy.
Wait until you can manage a silent retreat before starting at all.
Choose a clean, quiet corner, sit upright on a steady seat, and keep your normal meals and sleep.
apply.why: In 6.11-6.13 Krishna describes a clean spot, a steady seat and an upright posture, and in 6.16 he says yoga is not for those who eat or sleep too much or too little.

6-3.reflect: What small corner or time of day could become your quiet place?
6-3.practice: Sit upright for three minutes in a clean, quiet spot and rest your attention gently on your breath.

6-4.title: A lamp where no wind blows
6-4.teaching: Moderation in food, rest, work and sleep is what allows practice to ease suffering. A settled mind is like a lamp in a windless place: its flame stays still. In that stillness you find a deep joy that does not depend on outside things.
6-4.keyIdea: A balanced life lets the mind glow like a lamp without wind.

apply.scenario: You are building a side business and have been working until 2 a.m., skipping meals, then crashing all weekend. You feel anxious and scattered.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Push even harder for a few months; balance can come after you succeed.
Set regular times for meals, work, a short break and sleep so your mind can settle.
Give up the business, since it is clearly too stressful for you.
Rely on energy drinks during the week and sleep all weekend to recover.
apply.why: In 6.17 Krishna says yoga removes suffering for one who is moderate in eating, recreation, work, sleep and waking.

6-4.reflect: Where in your daily routine are you swinging between too much and too little?
6-4.practice: Pick one fixed bedtime for tonight and keep it.

6-5.title: Gently bring the mind back
6-5.teaching: Yoga is the art of unhooking from suffering, practiced with determination and without losing heart. Progress comes little by little. Whenever the mind wanders, for any reason, you simply bring it back, again and again.
6-5.keyIdea: Every time you bring the wandering mind back, you are doing it right.

apply.scenario: You sit for ten quiet minutes before bed, but your mind keeps jumping to tomorrow's job interview and you start to feel you are bad at this.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Give up; some people's minds just aren't made for quiet sitting.
Force your mind to go blank and get annoyed each time a thought appears.
Each time you notice the mind has wandered, gently bring it back and keep going, little by little.
Switch to a different technique every night until one feels effortless.
apply.why: In 6.26 Krishna says that whenever the restless mind wanders, we should simply bring it back, and 6.25 adds that steadiness comes little by little.

6-5.reflect: How do you usually speak to yourself when your attention slips?
6-5.practice: Count ten breaths; each time you lose count, smile and start again at one.

6-6.title: See yourself in everyone
6-6.teaching: As the mind grows calm, a deep joy arises, and with it a new way of seeing: the same Self lives in every being. Whoever sees Krishna everywhere is never apart from him, whatever their outer life looks like.
6-6.keyIdea: The same Self lives in every being, even the ones you find difficult.

apply.scenario: A cousin you have always found annoying is staying with your family for a week, and you are tempted to hide in your room the whole time.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Stay polite but distant; you don't have to connect with everyone.
Complain to your parents until they shorten the visit.
Spend time together but quietly count the hours until they leave.
Look for the same hopes, fears and goodness in them that you have, and spend some real time together.
apply.why: In 6.29 Krishna says a person steadied by yoga sees the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, looking on everyone with an equal eye.

6-6.reflect: Who in your life is hardest to see as 'like you', and what might you have in common?
6-6.practice: Today, silently wish one person you find difficult: 'May you be well.'

6-7.title: The restless mind can be trained
6-7.teaching: The highest yogi feels others' joy and pain as their own. Arjuna honestly admits his mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and Krishna agrees, but says practice and letting go can train it. With the right methods, steady effort works.
6-7.keyIdea: The mind is restless like the wind, yet practice and letting go steady it.

apply.scenario: You reach for your phone every few minutes while working, and you have started to believe you are just 'a distracted person' who can't change.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Accept it; some minds are simply wired to be scattered.
Admit it's hard, then practice short daily focus sessions and gently loosen your pull toward the phone.
Delete every app in one dramatic move and hope your willpower holds.
Wait until you feel naturally motivated before trying to focus again.
apply.why: In 6.35 Krishna agrees the mind is restless and hard to control, but says it can be trained through steady practice and detachment.

6-7.reflect: What habit of mind have you assumed you can never change?
6-7.practice: Put your phone in another room for one 25-minute focus session today.

6-8.title: Sincere effort is never wasted
6-8.teaching: Arjuna fears that someone who tries and falls short loses everything. Krishna reassures him warmly: no one who does good ever comes to a bad end. Even unfinished effort carries forward and opens better chances to grow.
6-8.keyIdea: No one who does good ever comes to a bad end.

apply.scenario: You spent two years training for a career that didn't work out. Now you feel those years were wasted and that you have fallen behind everyone.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Recognize that the effort, skills and character you built still count, and carry them into what comes next.
Conclude it was a mistake to try and play it safe from now on.
Leave those two years off your resume and avoid mentioning them to friends.
Work twice as hard to make up for the 'lost' time as quickly as possible.
apply.why: In 6.40 Krishna tells Arjuna that one who does good never comes to grief, in this world or the next.

6-8.reflect: What past effort that 'didn't work out' has quietly shaped who you are now?
6-8.practice: Write down three things you gained from an effort you once thought was a failure.

6-9.title: Keep going; growth adds up
6-9.teaching: Good practice is never lost: it returns and carries you forward, sometimes almost on its own. Growth builds over time. Krishna urges Arjuna to be a yogi and says the dearest is one who practices with faith and a loving heart.
6-9.keyIdea: Every sincere step you take keeps carrying you forward.

apply.scenario: You played the guitar every day as a teenager but stopped for years. Picking it up again, you wonder whether it is pointless to start over.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Don't bother; you've lost too much ground to ever catch up.
Only restart if you can practice three hours a day like you used to.
Start again with heart; your earlier practice will come back faster than you expect.
Read about guitar technique online instead of actually playing.
apply.why: In 6.43-6.44 Krishna says the understanding gained before comes back, and earlier practice carries a person forward almost by itself.

6-9.reflect: What practice in your life is waiting for you to come back to it?
6-9.practice: Spend ten minutes today on one good practice you have let slip.

7-1.title: Look beneath the surface
7-1.teaching: Krishna offers knowledge that is lived, not just learned. Body, mind and even ego belong to the changing, outer layer of nature. Beneath it is a deeper, living spirit that holds everything up, and that is worth seeking sincerely.
7-1.keyIdea: You are more than your body, thoughts and image; life itself flows through you.

apply.scenario: Your posts get fewer likes than your friends', and lately your mood rises and falls with the numbers. You have started to feel worthless.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Post more often and copy trending styles until the numbers go up.
Remember that looks, opinions and image are only the surface, and nurture the deeper life within you.
Delete your accounts in anger and tell everyone social media is fake.
Compare your stats with your friends' every week to see where you stand.
apply.why: In 7.4-7.5 Krishna explains that body, mind and ego belong to his changing lower nature, while the deeper life that sustains everything is his higher nature.

7-1.reflect: What part of you stays the same no matter how others see you?
7-1.practice: Before checking your phone this morning, take one minute simply to notice that you are alive.

7-2.title: See the sacred in ordinary things
7-2.teaching: Everything is strung on the divine like pearls on a thread. Krishna points to himself in the taste of water, the light of the sun and moon, the fragrance of the earth, the life in living things and the intelligence of the wise. Ordinary moments can become reminders of something sacred.
7-2.keyIdea: The divine is the taste in water and the light in the sun.

apply.scenario: Your days feel gray and repetitive: commute, work, dinner, sleep. It seems life only really happens on holidays.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Plan your next holiday and simply endure the weeks until then.
Fill every spare moment with shows and scrolling to escape the boredom.
Accept that this flatness is just what adult life is like.
Pause in ordinary moments, like drinking water or feeling sunlight, and notice them as gifts from a deeper source.
apply.why: In 7.8 Krishna says he is the taste in water and the light of the sun and moon, so even everyday things can point to the sacred.

7-2.reflect: Where in an ordinary day have you felt a quiet sense of wonder?
7-2.practice: Drink one glass of water slowly today, really tasting it, with a moment of thanks.

7-3.title: Strength without greed
7-3.teaching: Krishna is the strength that is free from greed, and the desire that stays in harmony with what is right. All moods of nature, calm, restless or dull, come from him, but he is not caught in them. Illusion is hard to see through alone, yet turning toward the divine helps us cross it.
7-3.keyIdea: True strength is free of greed; good desire serves what is right.

apply.scenario: You are the strongest negotiator on your team. You could pressure a small supplier into an unfairly low price and earn yourself a bonus.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Use your skill to reach a fair deal that is good for both sides, even if your bonus is smaller.
Push the supplier as hard as you can; business is business.
Let your manager decide so it isn't your responsibility.
Take the low price this time and promise yourself you'll be fair next time.
apply.why: In 7.11 Krishna says he is the strength of the strong that is free from greed and attachment, and desire that does not go against dharma (what is right).

7-3.reflect: Which of your desires feel in harmony with what is right, and which pull against it?
7-3.practice: Use one of your strengths today to help someone, expecting nothing in return.

7-4.title: Every sincere seeker is welcome
7-4.teaching: People turn to the divine for different reasons: pain, curiosity, needs or wisdom. Krishna calls them all noble, while the wise who love him for his own sake are especially dear. When desires cloud our wisdom, we settle for smaller goals.
7-4.keyIdea: Whether you come in pain, curiosity or need, you are welcome.

apply.scenario: Your friend has started praying since her father fell ill. Another friend teases her for 'only turning to God when she's desperate'.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Agree with the teasing friend; faith that starts in a crisis isn't sincere.
Stay silent so you don't have to take sides.
Gently say that turning to the divine in hard times is real and honorable, and stand by her.
Tell her she should study religion properly before she starts praying.
apply.why: In 7.16-7.18 Krishna names the distressed among the four kinds of people who turn to him, and calls all of them noble.

7-4.reflect: What first drew you to questions of meaning or faith, and how has your reason changed over time?
7-4.practice: Write one honest sentence about what you are truly seeking in life right now.

7-5.title: Honor faith, seek what lasts
7-5.teaching: Krishna steadies anyone's sincere faith, whatever form they worship, and he is the one who grants its fruits. But rewards sought only for limited wishes do not last. The deepest reality is unborn and unchanging, greater than any single form we picture.
7-5.keyIdea: Sincere faith is always supported; seek what lasts, not only what passes.

apply.scenario: At a family gathering, relatives from different faith traditions start arguing about whose way of worship is the 'right' one.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Join in and defend your own tradition as the only real one.
Declare that all religion is pointless so the argument ends.
Leave the room and avoid these relatives in the future.
Respect each person's sincere faith, and gently steer the talk toward the deeper, lasting good each one seeks.
apply.why: In 7.21 Krishna says that whatever form a person worships with faith, he himself makes that faith steady, and 7.23 notes that limited aims bring limited fruits.

7-5.reflect: What do you hope your faith or values will bring you: something passing, or something lasting?
7-5.practice: Ask someone today what their faith or values mean to them, and simply listen.

7-6.title: Loosen your likes and dislikes
7-6.teaching: From birth we are pulled by opposites: liking and disliking, wanting and avoiding. Those who live well and loosen this pull find steady devotion. Taking refuge in the divine brings understanding of the true Self and a mind that stays steady, even at the very end.
7-6.keyIdea: Likes and dislikes color everything; loosen their grip and see clearly.

apply.scenario: A new teammate has a manner you disliked from day one, and you have noticed you dismiss every idea they suggest.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Notice your dislike, set it aside, and judge their ideas on their own merits.
Trust your gut; first impressions are usually right.
Avoid working with them so there is no conflict.
Pretend to agree with their ideas so you seem open-minded.
apply.why: In 7.27 Krishna says all beings are confused by the pairs of opposites born of desire and aversion, and in 7.28 the steady ones are those freed from that confusion.

7-6.reflect: Which of your strong dislikes might be shaping how you see someone unfairly?
7-6.practice: Catch one instant 'I don't like that' today and ask: is this true, or just habit?

8-1.title: Ask the big questions
8-1.teaching: Arjuna is not afraid to ask the deepest questions about the self, action and the end of life. Krishna answers calmly and patiently: the infinite is imperishable, our true nature is the Self, and the divine lives within us. Remembering him brings peace, even at life's close.
8-1.keyIdea: Big questions are welcome; asking them is the start of wisdom.

apply.scenario: Your elderly grandfather has started talking openly about death and what might come after. It makes you uneasy, and you usually change the subject.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Change the subject quickly; talking about it will only make him sad.
Tell him not to think about such things yet.
Listen calmly, ask what gives him peace, and share your own questions too.
Look up life expectancy figures online to reassure him.
apply.why: In 8.1-8.2 Arjuna openly asks about the Self, action and the time of death, and in 8.3-8.5 Krishna answers calmly, offering peace rather than fear.

8-1.reflect: Which big question about life have you wondered about but never asked out loud?
8-1.practice: Write down one deep question you carry, without needing an answer yet.

8-2.title: What you practice, you become
8-2.teaching: What we think about most fills our mind at the moments that matter. So Krishna tells Arjuna to remember him always and to do his work. Spiritual life is not separate from daily duty; it is a steady thread running through it.
8-2.keyIdea: Keep what is sacred in mind while you do your daily work.

apply.scenario: Your days are packed with work and family duties, and you feel there is no room for anything spiritual until you retire.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Keep a quiet remembrance of what is sacred running through your day while doing your work well.
Postpone any spiritual practice until retirement, when life will be calmer.
Cut back on work and family duties to make time for long retreats.
Feel guilty about it now and then, but carry on exactly as usual.
apply.why: In 8.7 Krishna tells Arjuna to remember him at all times and also to fight, joining inner remembrance with daily duty.

8-2.reflect: What thoughts fill your mind most often on an ordinary day?
8-2.practice: Choose one daily cue, like opening a door, to pause and recall what matters most.

8-3.title: Steady remembrance makes it easy
8-3.teaching: Krishna describes deep meditation and the sacred sound Om. But his clearest promise is simple: he is easy to reach for anyone who remembers him steadily, day after day. Consistency matters more than dramatic effort.
8-3.keyIdea: Daily, steady remembrance makes the divine easy to reach.

apply.scenario: You feel far from your inner life. A friend suggests a ten-day silent retreat next year, and you wonder what to do until then.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Wait for the retreat; until then there is little point in trying.
Begin a short daily practice now, like a few minutes of prayer or quietly repeating Om, and keep it steady.
Read as many spiritual books as you can this month to catch up.
Do one intense three-hour session this weekend, then rest for a few weeks.
apply.why: In 8.14 Krishna says he is easily reached by one who remembers him constantly, day after day, with a focused mind.

8-3.reflect: What would a small, daily act of remembrance look like in your life?
8-3.practice: Sit quietly for two minutes and softly repeat 'Om', aloud or silently, feeling its calm.

8-4.title: Everything moves in cycles
8-4.teaching: Everything in this world, even the highest heavens, comes and goes in vast cycles of cosmic day and night. Seeing this big picture puts our worries in perspective. What lasts is the connection with Krishna, which lies beyond the cycle.
8-4.keyIdea: Everything comes and goes; anchor yourself in what does not.

apply.scenario: Your savings shrank sharply when the market fell. You can't sleep and keep checking the numbers, feeling as if your whole future is collapsing.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Check the numbers every hour so you are never caught off guard again.
Decide that nothing you build matters, since it can all disappear.
Blame yourself constantly for not seeing it coming.
Remember that worldly things rise and fall in cycles, take sensible steps, and anchor your peace in what lasts.
apply.why: In 8.16-8.19 Krishna explains that all worlds and beings come and go in cycles, while reaching him lies beyond that coming and going.

8-4.reflect: What in your life feels permanent but is really part of a cycle?
8-4.practice: Look at the night sky, or a photo of space, for one minute and feel the bigger picture.

8-5.title: Love is the way home
8-5.teaching: Beyond everything that appears and disappears is an eternal reality that is never destroyed. Krishna calls it his supreme home. It is reached not by cleverness but by wholehearted devotion to the one in whom all beings live.
8-5.keyIdea: The eternal is reached by a wholehearted, loving heart.

apply.scenario: Since your mother passed away, you feel anxious that everything and everyone you love will eventually slip away.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Take comfort that beneath all change is an eternal reality, and let love keep you connected to it.
Stay so busy that you never have time to think about it.
Avoid getting close to anyone so it won't hurt this much again.
Tell yourself grief is weakness and push the feelings down.
apply.why: In 8.20 Krishna says there is an eternal reality that is not destroyed when all beings pass, and in 8.22 that it is reached through wholehearted devotion.

8-5.reflect: What do you love that feels connected to something beyond time?
8-5.practice: Spend a few quiet minutes with a loving memory of someone you miss, breathing gently.

8-6.title: Stay steady, whatever the timing
8-6.teaching: Krishna describes a bright path that leads beyond return and a dark path that leads back. Rather than worrying about these, he says the one who understands them is not confused: simply stay steady in yoga at all times. That steady practice goes further than study, ritual or charity alone.
8-6.keyIdea: Don't wait for the perfect moment; stay steady in practice every day.

apply.scenario: You keep postponing a healthier routine, waiting for the 'perfect' moment: a new month, a holiday, your birthday.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Wait for the first of next month, when it will feel like a proper fresh start.
Start nothing until your schedule is completely clear.
Begin today with one small, steady step; constant practice matters more than perfect timing.
Write a list of ten new habits to launch all at once on your birthday.
apply.why: In 8.27 Krishna says the yogi who understands these paths is not confused by them, and urges Arjuna to be steady in yoga at all times.

8-6.reflect: What have you been waiting for the 'right time' to begin?
8-6.practice: Take one small step today toward something you have been putting off.

9-1.title: Wisdom you can actually live
9-1.teaching: Krishna shares his deepest teaching with someone who listens with an open heart. This wisdom is not just information; it is something you can experience and practise, and it gets easier and more joyful as you go.
9-1.keyIdea: The deepest wisdom is meant to be lived, not just learned.

apply.scenario: Your friend recommends a meditation practice that helped her a lot. Part of you wants to dismiss it as hype before even trying.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Dismiss it; most of these things are just trends anyway.
Research every criticism online first until you feel sure.
Listen openly, try it sincerely for a while, and judge from your own experience.
Agree politely but never actually try it.
apply.why: In 9.1-9.2 Krishna shares his teaching with one who does not scoff, and calls it knowledge that can be directly experienced and is joyful to practise.

9-1.reflect: Where in your life might a little less cynicism open the door to something good?
9-1.practice: Pick one piece of wisdom you already know and actually practise it once today.

9-2.title: Held by something larger
9-2.teaching: Krishna says all beings move within the Divine the way wind always moves within the sky. Nature does its work in great cycles, and the Divine acts without being tangled in it. You are part of a vast, steady order.
9-2.keyIdea: Like wind in the sky, you always move within something larger.

apply.scenario: Your whole week feels chaotic: deadlines, family errands, a sick pet. You feel like everything depends on you holding it together.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Remember you are held within a larger order; do your part calmly without carrying the whole universe.
Push harder and cancel all rest until everything is under control.
Give up on the week since nothing is going right.
Complain to everyone so they understand how much you are carrying.
apply.why: In 9.6 Krishna says all beings rest in him like wind in the sky, and in 9.9-9.10 he describes acting without being bound, while nature keeps the world turning.

9-2.reflect: What are you carrying as if it all depends on you alone?
9-2.practice: Step outside, feel the air moving, and remind yourself you are held by something larger.

9-3.title: The sacred in plain sight
9-3.teaching: People often miss the sacred when it appears in something ordinary and human. Those with open, generous hearts recognize it and respond with love, through praise, steady effort or seeking understanding.
9-3.keyIdea: The sacred often hides in the ordinary; open eyes can see it.

apply.scenario: Your grandmother quietly cooks for everyone every Sunday. You have always treated it as routine and barely noticed her effort.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Keep treating it as routine; that is just what grandmothers do.
Offer to pay her for the groceries so it is fair.
Recognize the love and care in her ordinary act and honour it with real gratitude.
Suggest ordering takeout so she does not have to bother.
apply.why: In 9.11 Krishna says people overlook the divine when it appears in a plain human form; in 9.13 great souls see deeper and respond with devotion.

9-3.reflect: Who or what have you been treating as ordinary that might deserve more reverence?
9-3.practice: Notice one everyday kindness today and thank the person specifically for it.

9-4.title: Friend, shelter and home
9-4.teaching: Krishna describes himself as everything in a sacred act and as father, mother, friend, shelter and home of the whole world. Even life and death, sun and rain, belong to this one presence. Nothing in your life is outside its care.
9-4.keyIdea: The Divine is your shelter, your friend and your home.

apply.scenario: You have just moved to a new city for work. You feel lonely and rootless, like nothing here belongs to you.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Stay in your room until it feels like home on its own.
Remember the sacred is present here too, as shelter and friend, and begin to see this place with that trust.
Plan to move back as soon as possible.
Fill every evening with distractions so you do not feel it.
apply.why: In 9.17-9.18 Krishna calls himself the friend, the shelter and the abode of all, present everywhere, so no place is truly outside his care.

9-4.reflect: Which word from Krishna's list (friend, shelter, witness, home) do you most need right now?
9-4.practice: Pick one word from 9.18 and repeat it quietly whenever you feel unsettled today.

9-5.title: Rewards that run out
9-5.teaching: Pleasures earned by chasing rewards are real but temporary; when they are used up, we start chasing again. Those who keep the Divine at the centre are cared for: what they need is supplied and what they have is protected.
9-5.keyIdea: Rewards run out; a steady heart is quietly cared for.

apply.scenario: You finally got the promotion you worked toward for two years. A month later the excitement is gone and you are already eyeing the next title.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Start chasing the next title right away to get that feeling back.
Decide ambition is pointless and stop trying at work.
Keep the promotion a secret so nobody expects more from you.
Notice that rewards fade, and root your sense of meaning in something steadier than the next title.
apply.why: In 9.21 Krishna says reward-based joys run out and people return to the cycle, while in 9.22 he cares for those whose minds rest steadily on him.

9-5.reflect: Which reward have you been chasing, and what do you hope it will finally give you?
9-5.practice: Write down one thing that brings you lasting peace, not just a quick high.

9-6.title: Small offerings, great love
9-6.teaching: Krishna gladly accepts the simplest gift, a leaf, a flower, a little water, when it is given with love. Anything you do, eat or give can become an offering, and living this way sets you free from anxious clinging to results.
9-6.keyIdea: It is not the size of the gift, but the love in it.

apply.scenario: Your best friend's birthday is coming. You are short on money and feel embarrassed that you cannot buy anything impressive.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Skip the birthday and apologize later.
Give something simple, like a handwritten note, offered with real care.
Borrow money to buy something expensive.
Send a quick generic text so it does not seem like a big deal.
apply.why: In 9.26 Krishna says he accepts even a leaf, a flower or a little water when it is offered with love: the heart matters, not the price.

9-6.reflect: What everyday task could you quietly turn into an offering of love?
9-6.practice: Before one meal or chore today, pause and offer it inwardly with gratitude.

9-7.title: No one is beyond return
9-7.teaching: Krishna says even someone who has gone badly wrong becomes good once they sincerely turn toward the Divine. Birth, background or past do not shut anyone out. Whoever turns their whole self toward love is never lost.
9-7.keyIdea: Your past does not decide your future; your turning does.

apply.scenario: Years ago you hurt people through choices you now regret. Now you want to volunteer and grow, but you feel too 'stained' to deserve a fresh start.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Accept that some people are simply beyond change.
Wait until you have punished yourself enough before trying.
Hide your past and pretend it never happened.
Make a sincere turn now; a wholehearted new direction counts more than old mistakes.
apply.why: In 9.30-9.31 Krishna says even one who has done much wrong, turning to him sincerely, is to be seen as good and soon finds lasting peace.

9-7.reflect: Is there someone, maybe yourself, you have written off who deserves a second chance?
9-7.practice: Take one small step today in the direction of the person you want to become.

10-1.title: Every quality has one source
10-1.teaching: Krishna says even the gods cannot fully grasp where he comes from, because he is the source of all. Our understanding, forgiveness, calm, courage, joy and sorrow all arise from that one source. Seeing this helps us hold our inner life with less ego and more gratitude.
10-1.keyIdea: Your best qualities are gifts flowing from one source.

apply.scenario: Your coach praises your calm under pressure in a big match. You feel tempted to brag that you are simply better than your teammates.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Brag a little; you earned it.
Downplay it and insist you were just lucky.
Accept the praise with gratitude, seeing calm and skill as gifts that come from a deeper source.
Change the subject so nobody notices you.
apply.why: In 10.4-10.5 Krishna says qualities like intelligence, self-control and calm arise from him alone, so gratitude fits better than pride.

10-1.reflect: Which of your strengths could you hold as a gift rather than a trophy?
10-1.practice: Thank someone or something for a quality you have that you did not create alone.

10-2.title: Wisdom grows in good company
10-2.teaching: Those who see the Divine as the source of everything find joy in talking about it with each other, lighting up each other's understanding. To those who stay steady in love, Krishna gives the inner wisdom to find their way.
10-2.keyIdea: Share what inspires you; wisdom grows when it is shared.

apply.scenario: You have found a book that is changing how you see life. Your study group mostly talks about gossip and grades.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Gently share what you are learning and seek out friends who enjoy such conversations too.
Keep it to yourself; people will think you are weird.
Lecture your group until they agree it is important.
Quit the study group since they are not deep enough.
apply.why: In 10.9 Krishna describes devoted people enlightening one another and finding joy in speaking of the Divine together.

10-2.reflect: Who in your life helps you see more clearly, and do you tell them?
10-2.practice: Share one inspiring idea with a friend today and ask what inspires them.

10-3.title: A lamp lit from within
10-3.teaching: Out of compassion, Krishna lights a lamp of knowledge in the heart that clears away confusion. Arjuna responds with humble trust and asks to understand more. Clarity often comes when we are open and keep asking honestly.
10-3.keyIdea: Light one lamp of understanding and the darkness begins to lift.

apply.scenario: You have felt confused for weeks about which college major to pick. Everyone gives different advice and your mind feels foggy.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Pick at random just to end the stress.
Let your parents decide so it is not your responsibility.
Ignore the question until the deadline forces you.
Get quiet, ask honestly, and trust that clarity can arise from within as you stay open.
apply.why: In 10.11 Krishna says that, dwelling within the heart, he destroys the darkness of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.

10-3.reflect: What question are you ready to ask more honestly, instead of rushing to an answer?
10-3.practice: Sit quietly for five minutes, hold one question in mind, and simply listen.

10-4.title: Where can I find you?
10-4.teaching: Arjuna asks a beautiful question: in which things should I think of you? Krishna starts with the heart of every being, then with whatever shines brightest, like the sun. Remembering the sacred is easier when we connect it to things we already see.
10-4.keyIdea: Begin with the heart, then see the sacred in what shines.

apply.scenario: You want to feel more spiritually connected, but your days are packed with work and kids, leaving no time for long practices.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Wait until retirement when you will have more time.
Use what is already around you, like sunrise or a loved one's face, as reminders of the sacred.
Force yourself into a two-hour daily routine you cannot keep.
Decide spirituality just is not for busy people.
apply.why: In 10.17 Arjuna asks in what things to think of Krishna, and in 10.20-10.21 Krishna points to the Self in every heart and the radiant sun.

10-4.reflect: What everyday sight could become your reminder of something sacred?
10-4.practice: Notice the sun or sky once today and let it remind you of the Divine.

10-5.title: Greatness in quiet things
10-5.teaching: Krishna names himself as the mind among the senses, Om among sounds, silent repetition among offerings, and the Himalayas among mountains. The sacred often shows up as steadiness, stillness and awareness, not just noise and display.
10-5.keyIdea: The Divine often speaks through stillness, steadiness and awareness.

apply.scenario: You feel pressure to post constantly online to prove your life is exciting. Your quiet morning walks feel 'too boring' to count.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Post more often so you do not fall behind your friends.
Skip the walks and do something more impressive.
Delete all your accounts in frustration.
Value the quiet walks; stillness and steady awareness can be among the most sacred things.
apply.why: In 10.25 Krishna names himself as the silent repetition among offerings and the unmoving Himalayas, honouring stillness and steadiness.

10-5.reflect: Where in your life does stillness feel most meaningful?
10-5.practice: Spend three minutes in silence today, without your phone, simply breathing.

10-6.title: Look for the best in each
10-6.teaching: Krishna keeps naming the finest in each group: the lion among animals, the Ganga among rivers, Rama among warriors, honest reasoning in debate. Even Prahlada, a devoted soul born among demons, shows that goodness can shine anywhere.
10-6.keyIdea: In every group, look for the best; it points to the sacred.

apply.scenario: A new colleague comes from a team everyone at work complains about. Your friends assume she will be difficult too.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Look for her real strengths and goodness; excellence can appear anywhere.
Keep your distance just to be safe.
Go along with the group's opinion to fit in.
Test her with a hard task to see if she fails.
apply.why: In 10.30 Krishna names himself as Prahlada among the demons, a reminder that goodness can shine even where we least expect it.

10-6.reflect: Who have you judged by their group rather than by who they are?
10-6.practice: Find and name one genuine strength in someone you usually overlook.

10-7.title: Time, spring and resolve
10-7.teaching: Krishna is endless time, the season of flowers, determination in the resolute and goodness in the good. Every ability, even cleverness, has one source, so the real question is how we use our gifts. Arjuna himself is named among the glories.
10-7.keyIdea: Every gift comes from one source; use yours for good.

apply.scenario: You are naturally persuasive. A classmate asks you to help talk the teacher into accepting work that was copied.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Help; being persuasive is your talent, so use it.
Stay out of it and say nothing either way.
Decline kindly and use your persuasiveness for something good, like helping them ask for an extension honestly.
Report them immediately without talking to them.
apply.why: In 10.36 Krishna names himself as resolve and the goodness of the good: our abilities flow from one source, and we are invited to use them well.

10-7.reflect: Which of your gifts could you use more intentionally for good?
10-7.practice: Use one of your talents today to help someone without being asked.

10-8.title: A spark of splendour everywhere
10-8.teaching: Krishna says his glories are endless and that whatever is beautiful, powerful or excellent is a spark of his splendour. The point is not memorising the list, but learning to feel awe wherever greatness appears.
10-8.keyIdea: Wherever you see splendour, you are glimpsing a spark of the Divine.

apply.scenario: You watch a friend play a stunning piano piece. Your first thought is envy because you could never play like that.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Avoid their concerts so you do not feel bad.
Point out their mistakes to feel better.
Decide you are simply untalented and stop trying music.
Let the beauty move you with wonder, seeing it as a spark of something sacred.
apply.why: In 10.41 Krishna says whatever is glorious or beautiful comes from a spark of his splendour, so awe fits better than envy.

10-8.reflect: When did you last feel genuine wonder at someone else's gift?
10-8.practice: Notice one beautiful thing today and pause long enough to feel awe.

11-1.title: Asking humbly to see more
11-1.teaching: Arjuna's confusion has lifted, and now he longs to experience the truth, not just hear about it. Yet he asks humbly: show me, if you think I can. Genuine seeking combines eagerness with humility.

apply.scenario: You admire a senior engineer at your company and want her to mentor you. You are tempted to demand a weekly slot because you feel you deserve it.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Demand the slot; if you do not push, you will not get anything.
Ask sincerely and humbly, explaining your interest, and leave the decision to her.
Avoid asking at all in case she says no.
Complain to your manager that nobody mentors you.
apply.why: In 11.4 Arjuna asks to see Krishna's form only 'if you think it possible for me', showing eager but humble seeking.

11-1.reflect: Is there something you want so much that you have forgotten to ask for it humbly?
11-1.practice: Make one request today with genuine humility and openness to either answer.

11-2.title: A new way of seeing
11-2.teaching: Krishna tells Arjuna that ordinary eyes cannot see the vast truth, so he gives him a divine eye. Some things can only be understood when we change how we look, not just how hard we stare.
11-2.keyIdea: Sometimes you need new eyes, not more effort.

apply.scenario: You and your sister keep arguing about caring for your ageing parents. Each of you is sure the other is being unfair.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Try to see the situation through a wider lens, including her view, before deciding who is right.
Collect more evidence to prove you are right.
Stop talking to her until she apologizes.
Let her handle everything so you can avoid the conflict.
apply.why: In 11.8 Krishna says Arjuna cannot see the truth with ordinary eyes and gives him a divine eye: a changed way of seeing.

11-2.reflect: Where might a different way of seeing change a struggle you are in?
11-2.practice: Pick one disagreement and write it from the other person's point of view.

11-3.title: Brighter than a thousand suns
11-3.teaching: Arjuna sees the whole universe gathered in one, shining brighter than a thousand suns. His natural response is wonder, bowing his head with folded hands. Awe makes us humble and opens our hearts.
11-3.keyIdea: Let wonder bring you to your knees, gently.

apply.scenario: On a camping trip you see the night sky full of stars for the first time. Your friends are busy taking selfies and checking signal.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Join the selfies; you can look at stars later online.
Complain that there is no signal out here.
Pause in silence and let the wonder of the vast sky humble and fill you.
Explain the astronomy to everyone so you seem smart.
apply.why: In 11.12-11.14 Arjuna sees a splendour like a thousand suns and, filled with wonder, bows with joined palms.

11-3.reflect: When did you last feel truly small in a good way?
11-3.practice: Look up at the sky for one full minute tonight without your phone.

11-4.title: No edges, no end
11-4.teaching: Arjuna sees a form with no beginning, middle or end, filling all space, with the sun and moon as its eyes. The infinite cannot be measured, and that can make our worries seem smaller and less permanent.
11-4.keyIdea: Before the infinite, your worries shrink to their true size.

apply.scenario: You failed an important exam and feel your whole future is ruined. You cannot stop replaying it.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Decide you are a failure and stop studying.
Hide the result from everyone.
Blame the teacher for unfair questions.
Step back and see this moment as one small part of a vast life; learn from it and keep going.
apply.why: In 11.16-11.19 Arjuna sees a reality without beginning, middle or end, putting any single moment into a much larger frame.

11-4.reflect: How big does today's worry look when you picture your whole life?
11-4.practice: Write today's biggest worry, then one sentence on how it might look in five years.

11-5.title: Honest about being overwhelmed
11-5.teaching: Faced with the immense vision, Arjuna admits he has lost his courage and peace, and asks for mercy. It is okay to feel overwhelmed by life's vastness. Naming it honestly and asking for grace is a humble response.
11-5.keyIdea: It is brave to admit you are overwhelmed and ask for help.

apply.scenario: Your newborn has not slept properly in weeks. You feel completely out of your depth but keep telling everyone you are fine.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Keep saying you are fine so nobody worries.
Admit honestly that you are overwhelmed and ask for support.
Assume other parents cope better and you are failing.
Push through alone; asking for help is weakness.
apply.why: In 11.24-11.25 Arjuna openly says he has lost his courage and peace and asks Krishna for mercy.

11-5.reflect: What are you carrying that you have not yet admitted is too heavy?
11-5.practice: Tell one trusted person honestly how you are really doing today.

11-6.title: Rivers flowing to the sea
11-6.teaching: Arjuna sees all beings, even the mightiest, flowing into the form like rivers into the ocean. It is a calm, awe-filled picture of time: everything changes and moves on. Seeing this helps us hold life more lightly and more preciously.
11-6.keyIdea: Like rivers to the sea, all things move on; cherish them now.

apply.scenario: Your old childhood home is being sold. You feel a deep ache, as though losing it erases your past.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Accept that all things move on like rivers to the sea, and cherish the memories with gratitude.
Try to stop the sale at any cost.
Refuse to visit one last time because it hurts.
Pretend it does not matter to you at all.
apply.why: In 11.28 Arjuna sees beings flowing into Krishna like rivers rushing to the ocean, an image of time carrying all things onward.

11-6.reflect: What in your life is changing, and how might you honour it as it goes?
11-6.practice: Write down one memory you are grateful for that belongs to a past season.

11-7.title: Be the instrument
11-7.teaching: Krishna reveals himself as Time, the force that moves all things to their completion. He tells Arjuna to rise and do his part as an instrument. We act fully, but we do not have to carry the weight of controlling every outcome.
11-7.keyIdea: Do your part fully; you are not in charge of everything.

apply.scenario: You are leading a community fundraiser. Many factors are outside your control and you lie awake worrying it will flop.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Cancel it so you cannot be blamed if it fails.
Micromanage every volunteer until it is perfect.
Give your best effort as your part, and trust the outcome to the larger flow of things.
Let someone else run it so the stress is theirs.
apply.why: In 11.33 Krishna tells Arjuna to rise and act, being 'merely an instrument', because the outcome lies in larger hands.

11-7.reflect: Which outcome are you trying to control that is not fully yours to control?
11-7.practice: Before one task today, say: I will do my part well and let go of the rest.

11-8.title: Reverence on every side
11-8.teaching: Overflowing with awe, Arjuna praises Krishna as the source of everything and bows in front, behind and on every side. When we sense the sacred in all directions, gratitude and reverence fill our whole life.
11-8.keyIdea: When the sacred is everywhere, reverence can be too.

apply.scenario: Life is going well: good health, a stable job, kind friends. Lately you have started taking it all for granted.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Enjoy it while it lasts and not think too much.
Worry that it will all fall apart soon.
Focus on what you still do not have.
Turn your attention to gratitude, honouring the many sources of good around you.
apply.why: In 11.39-11.40 Arjuna bows again and again, on every side, recognizing the Divine in everything around him.

11-8.reflect: What good things in your life have quietly become invisible to you?
11-8.practice: Name five things you are grateful for before you sleep tonight.

11-9.title: Forgiveness between friends
11-9.teaching: Arjuna realizes he sometimes treated Krishna too casually, as just a buddy, and asks forgiveness as a friend forgives a friend. Seeing someone's true worth invites us to own our carelessness and trust in loving forgiveness.
11-9.keyIdea: Own your carelessness; love makes room for forgiveness.

apply.scenario: Your longtime friend always shows up for you. You realize you have joked about her in ways that were careless and a bit dismissive.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Say nothing; she probably did not notice.
Sincerely acknowledge it, apologize, and appreciate her more deeply from now on.
Make it up to her with a gift instead of talking about it.
Distance yourself because you feel embarrassed.
apply.why: In 11.41-11.44 Arjuna admits he treated Krishna carelessly as merely a friend and asks forgiveness as a friend forgives a friend.

11-9.reflect: Who in your life might you have taken for granted because they are so familiar?
11-9.practice: Send a short message of real appreciation to someone you often take for granted.

11-10.title: Comfort after the storm
11-10.teaching: After the overwhelming vision, Arjuna asks to see Krishna's gentle form again, and Krishna lovingly reassures him: do not be afraid. The Divine is both vast and tender, and it is fine to need comfort after facing something huge.
11-10.keyIdea: After facing something vast, it is okay to seek gentle comfort.

apply.scenario: You just got through a frightening health scare, and the test results were fine. You still feel shaken and a bit embarrassed by it.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Push the feelings away and get straight back to work.
Keep researching worst-case scenarios online.
Accept that you are shaken, and let yourself be comforted by familiar people and routines.
Tell yourself you were silly to be scared at all.
apply.why: In 11.49-11.50 Krishna tells the shaken Arjuna not to fear, returns to his gentle form and consoles him.

11-10.reflect: What gentle, familiar things bring you back to yourself after a hard time?
11-10.practice: Do one comforting, familiar thing for yourself today, without guilt.

11-11.title: Love opens every door
11-11.teaching: Krishna says study, ritual, charity and discipline alone cannot reveal him; wholehearted love can. Those who act for the highest, let go of clinging and hold no hatred toward any being come close to him.
11-11.keyIdea: Love, without hatred toward anyone, is the truest way in.

apply.scenario: Your neighbour was rude to you last month. You do good things every week but quietly hold a grudge against him.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Let go of the grudge and wish him well; real devotion includes no hatred toward any being.
Keep the grudge; he deserves it after being rude.
Do even more good deeds to balance out the grudge.
Tell other neighbours how rude he was.
apply.why: In 11.55 Krishna says the one who comes to him acts for the highest, loves and bears no enmity toward any creature.

11-11.reflect: Is there a small grudge you could begin to set down?
11-11.practice: Silently wish well to one person you find difficult today.

12-1.title: Choose a path you can walk
12-1.teaching: Arjuna asks which spiritual path is best, and Krishna honors both loving God in a personal form and seeking the formless. He gently notes that steady, wholehearted love is the more natural road for most embodied people. What matters is sincere focus and care for all beings.
12-1.keyIdea: The best path is the one you can walk with your whole heart.

apply.scenario: Your friend meditates in silence for an hour daily, while you feel closer to the sacred through prayer and music. You start wondering if your way is 'less spiritual'.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Force yourself into silent meditation, since harder paths must be better.
Drop spiritual practice altogether until you figure out the one correct method.
Keep your heartfelt practice steady and sincere; Krishna honors both paths and calls loving focus the easier road.
Try to convince your friend that your way is the superior one.
apply.why: In 12.2 Krishna praises those who worship him with steady faith, and in 12.5 he notes the formless path is harder for embodied beings, while 12.4 says both reach him.

12-1.reflect: Where do you most naturally feel connected to something larger than yourself?
12-1.practice: Spend five minutes today in whatever form of prayer, gratitude or quiet feels most natural to you.

12-2.title: A step that fits you
12-2.teaching: Krishna offers a ladder of options: fix your mind on him; if you cannot, practice; if that is hard, work as service; if even that is hard, let go of the results. Nobody is left out. You start from wherever you honestly are.
12-2.keyIdea: Can't do the big step? Take the smaller one sincerely.

apply.scenario: You keep trying to meditate for 30 minutes but give up after three days each time. You feel like spiritual growth just isn't for you.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Practice a little each day and gently return when your mind wanders; steady repetition is the path.
Accept that some people are spiritual and you simply aren't one of them.
Wait until life is calmer before attempting any practice at all.
Push harder and meditate for two hours to make up for the missed days.
apply.why: In 12.9 Krishna says that if the mind will not stay fixed, reach the goal through regular practice, and 12.10 offers even simpler steps.

12-2.reflect: Which step on Krishna's ladder feels honest and doable for you right now?
12-2.practice: Choose one task today and do it quietly as an offering, not for credit.

12-3.title: Letting go brings peace
12-3.teaching: Krishna says letting go of clinging to results is a powerful step, because peace follows immediately. He then describes people dear to him: free of hatred, friendly, compassionate, humble, forgiving, and hard to unsettle. They neither disturb the world nor are disturbed by it.
12-3.keyIdea: Do your best, release the result, and peace follows.

apply.scenario: A coworker took credit for a project you mostly did. You feel resentment rising and are drafting a sharp message to the whole team.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Send the sharp message now so everyone sees who really did the work.
Say nothing and quietly hold a grudge against the coworker.
Stop putting real effort into shared projects from now on.
Calmly clarify facts if needed, without hatred, and let go of needing credit to feel at peace.
apply.why: In 12.12 Krishna says peace follows letting go of results, and 12.13 describes his dear one as free of hatred, friendly, and forgiving.

12-3.reflect: What result are you holding so tightly that it is costing you your peace?
12-3.practice: Finish one task today, then consciously say to yourself: 'I did my part; I let it go.'

12-4.title: Steady in praise and blame
12-4.teaching: Krishna's dear ones stay the same through honor and insult, gain and loss, friend and critic. They expect little, act skillfully, and are content. This calm is not coldness; it is a love that does not depend on how life treats you.
12-4.keyIdea: Let praise and blame pass through you like weather.

apply.scenario: Your social media post got lots of praise yesterday, and today a harsh comment calls it stupid. Your mood keeps swinging with each notification.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Delete the post so nobody can criticize you again.
Notice both the praise and the insult without being ruled by either, and stay steady in your values.
Reply to the critic until they admit they were wrong.
Keep refreshing to collect more praise to cancel out the insult.
apply.why: In 12.18 and 12.19 Krishna says the one dear to him is the same in honor and dishonor and unmoved by praise or blame.

12-4.reflect: Whose praise or blame has the most power over your mood, and why?
12-4.practice: Next time you get a compliment or criticism today, pause and take three slow breaths before reacting.

13-1.title: You are more than your body
13-1.teaching: Krishna calls the body the 'field' (kshetra) and the awareness that knows it the 'knower of the field' (kshetrajna). Your body and mind change constantly, but there is a part of you that witnesses all of it. Real knowledge starts with seeing that difference.
13-1.keyIdea: The body is the field; you are the one who knows it.

apply.scenario: An injury means you can't play the sport you love for a whole season. You feel like you've lost who you are.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Decide that without your sport you are nobody, and withdraw from your friends.
Care for your body, but remember you are the aware self behind it, not only its abilities.
Ignore the doctor and keep playing so you don't lose your identity.
Distract yourself constantly so you never have to think about it.
apply.why: In 13.2 Krishna explains that the body is the field, and the one who knows the field is distinct from it.

13-1.reflect: What part of your identity do you tie most tightly to your body or abilities?
13-1.practice: Sit for one minute and simply notice sensations in your body, as a calm observer.

13-2.title: What wisdom looks like
13-2.teaching: Even desire, dislike, pleasure and pain are part of the changing 'field', not your core self. Krishna says wisdom shows up as character: humility, sincerity, non-harming, patience, honesty, and steadiness. Knowledge is measured by how you live, not by what you can recite.
13-2.keyIdea: Wisdom is humility, patience and honesty in daily life.

apply.scenario: At work you made an error in a report, and your manager hasn't noticed yet. Admitting it might make you look less capable.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Quietly fix it later and hope nobody ever asks.
Point out that a teammate also reviewed the report.
Leave it; small errors happen and aren't worth the embarrassment.
Admit the mistake simply and fix it, showing humility and honesty.
apply.why: In 13.8 Krishna lists humility, sincerity and uprightness as marks of true wisdom.

13-2.reflect: Which of Krishna's signs of wisdom (humility, patience, honesty, self-control) comes hardest for you?
13-2.practice: Today, own one small mistake out loud, without excuses.

13-3.title: Make room for quiet
13-3.teaching: Krishna includes a love of solitude and steady inner seeking in his list of wisdom. Without quiet time, we rarely hear ourselves think. He then describes the Supreme Reality as present everywhere, shining through every sense.
13-3.keyIdea: Inner growth needs some quiet space every day.

apply.scenario: From the moment you wake up until you sleep, there is always a podcast, a group chat or a video playing. You feel restless but can't say why.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Build in short daily periods of silence to reflect and turn inward.
Add more content, maybe self-help podcasts, to fill every gap productively.
Assume the restlessness is just modern life and accept it.
Go off-grid completely and cut off all your friends.
apply.why: In 13.11 and 13.12 Krishna names a love of solitude and constant seeking of self-knowledge as part of wisdom.

13-3.reflect: When was the last time you sat in silence, and what did you notice?
13-3.practice: Spend ten minutes today without any screen, music or talk, just with your thoughts.

13-4.title: The light in every heart
13-4.teaching: Krishna describes the Supreme as both far beyond us and closer than anything, inside and outside all beings. It is the 'light of lights', seated in every heart. Even when life feels dark, that light has not gone anywhere.
13-4.keyIdea: What feels far away is already seated in your heart.

apply.scenario: You've just moved to a new city for college and know no one. At night you feel deeply alone and cut off from everything familiar.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Conclude you made a mistake and plan to move back immediately.
Stay in your room until loneliness passes on its own.
Remember the light within is near even now, and from that steadiness reach out to others.
Fill the evenings with parties to drown the feeling out.
apply.why: In 13.16 Krishna says the Supreme is far yet near, and in 13.18 that it is the light of lights, seated in the hearts of all.

13-4.reflect: When have you felt an inner steadiness even in a hard or lonely moment?
13-4.practice: Before sleeping, place a hand on your heart and breathe slowly for one minute.

13-5.title: Watch from the witness seat
13-5.teaching: Nature (prakriti) drives the body and its actions, while the conscious self experiences pleasure and pain through attachment. Within us is also the Supreme Self, the silent witness. Stepping back into that witness view loosens the grip of strong reactions.
13-5.keyIdea: You can watch your emotions without being swept away by them.

apply.scenario: During a family dinner, your sibling brings up an old argument. You feel heat rising and words forming that you know will hurt.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Pause and observe the anger as a passing wave, then respond calmly.
Say the hurtful words; holding them in isn't healthy.
Leave the table without a word and refuse to talk for days.
Agree with everything just to avoid conflict, then complain later.
apply.why: In 13.23 Krishna calls the Self within the witness, and 13.21 shows pleasure and pain are experienced through our identification with nature.

13-5.reflect: What emotion most often 'grabs the wheel' from you, and what helps you step back?
13-5.practice: When a strong emotion rises today, silently name it: 'This is anger' or 'This is fear.'

13-6.title: See the same Spirit everywhere
13-6.teaching: Krishna says the one who sees the same Supreme in all beings, the undying within the dying, truly sees. This vision changes how we treat others and ourselves. Even people who simply trust what they have heard and follow it sincerely are on the path.
13-6.keyIdea: Truly seeing means seeing the same Spirit in everyone.

apply.scenario: A new student at school has a strong accent and some classmates mock him. Your friends expect you to laugh along.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Laugh along quietly so you don't become the next target.
Stay out of it; it isn't your problem.
Lecture your friends loudly in front of everyone about how bad they are.
Treat the new student with the same respect as anyone, seeing the same Spirit in him.
apply.why: In 13.28 Krishna says the one who sees the Supreme Lord equally in all beings truly sees, and 13.29 says this vision lifts us too.

13-6.reflect: Who do you find it hardest to see as sharing the same inner light as you?
13-6.practice: Greet someone you usually overlook today with genuine warmth.

13-7.title: Untouched like the open sky
13-7.teaching: Krishna compares the Self to space: present everywhere, yet nothing sticks to it. Like one sun lighting the whole world, awareness lights up all experience. Seeing the difference between the changing field and its knower is the road to freedom.
13-7.keyIdea: Like the sky, your deepest self is never stained.

apply.scenario: After a bad performance review, a manager calls you 'unreliable'. The word keeps replaying in your head, and you feel it defines you.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Agree that you're simply unreliable and lower your goals.
Learn from the feedback, while knowing your deepest self isn't stained by any label.
Insist the manager is wrong and dismiss the feedback completely.
Work nonstop for weeks until the manager praises you again.
apply.why: In 13.33 Krishna says the Self, like space, remains untainted though it dwells in the body.

13-7.reflect: Which label from others or from yourself has stuck to you, and is it really who you are?
13-7.practice: Look at the sky for one minute today and remember: clouds pass, the sky stays.

14-1.title: Three forces in your mind
14-1.teaching: Krishna says all life comes from nature joined with the divine, so every being shares one origin. Nature works through three qualities: sattva (clarity), rajas (restlessness) and tamas (dullness). These forces bind us, but understanding them is the start of freedom.
14-1.keyIdea: Know the three forces, and they lose their hidden grip.

apply.scenario: You notice your study days follow a pattern: foggy mornings, frantic afternoons cramming, and clear-headed evenings. You assume you're just a 'bad student'.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Accept the label 'bad student' and stop trying to improve.
Force yourself to study only in the mornings, since they feel worst.
See these as shifting qualities of nature, not your identity, and plan your work around them.
Rely on caffeine to stay in the frantic mode all day.
apply.why: In 14.5 Krishna explains that sattva, rajas and tamas are qualities of nature that bind the self; they are not the self.
